[{"uuid": "6104aa31-e838-45a4-a8b1-dd90c6808a5e", "name": "AI competition project architecture and multi-agent system design", "summary": "**Conversation Overview**\n\nThis conversation involved a student preparing a submission for the SLIIT Codefest 2026 AI Competition, specifically sub-track 1C (\"Searching the Way a Human Does\"), working under significant time pressure due to mid-semester exams throughout the build period. The person had prior experience building multi-agent systems with CrewAI for stock prediction and implementing RAG pipelines with Ollama, and explicitly asked Claude to act as both architect and examiner \u2014 designing and building the project step by step while the person tested locally and reported terminal output back. The person stated a strong preference for receiving complete files to paste rather than partial edits or zip files, and for keeping explanations simple enough to share with a friend with no coding background.\n\nThe project involved building an AI research agent over the Ashen Era Archive, a fictional fantasy corpus of 415 mixed-format files (markdown wiki articles, Word and PDF codexes and chronicles, in-world ephemera, and standalone images). The core architecture progressed through seven stages: format-agnostic ingestion with per-source reliability tiering, heading-based document splitting, table extraction, chunk embedding via OpenRouter's free embedding model into ChromaDB, a hybrid semantic-plus-keyword search tool, an iterative agent loop (search \u2192 read \u2192 decide: search again or answer, up to five iterations), and a separate conflict-resolution specialist agent invoked only when multiple sources disagreed. Key design decisions included dropping a planned 1B/1C combination in favor of a single strong 1C system, switching from Voyage AI and Grok to OpenRouter due to card constraints, replacing pandoc with native python-docx to eliminate a Windows system dependency, and deliberately disabling OCR for performance reasons documented as an intentional trade-off. Several real bugs were diagnosed and fixed throughout, always using actual terminal output as evidence rather than guessing: a format-versus-topic assumption that broke mixed-format folders, a heading-level cap that caused duplicate document IDs in the bestiary codex file, a blank forced-answer output when the agent exhausted its search iterations, and duplicate evidence titles printing five times per matched document.\n\nThe person worked through numerous Windows-specific environment issues (Tesseract PATH misconfiguration, stale Python bytecode caches, PowerShell multi-line paste behavior) and consistently caught Claude's mistakes, including an early testing gap where the system was validated on only one hand-picked question before UI work began, a docs folder named `doc` instead of the required `docs`, and Tesseract binary files accidentally committed to the git repository. Validated test results confirmed the system correctly answered both official 1C sample questions (Gloamreach founding year: 246 AS with a codex-over-ephemera conflict resolved; Gauntlet of Sorrowfell forging year: 391 AS with the same pattern), a self-generated multi-hop question (Ederon Fellgard \u2192 Iron-Ring Cartel \u2192 The Leaden Accord across two search steps), and an honest-uncertainty case (Ashreach flag hex color: \"insufficient evidence\" after five iterations). The 1B batch test produced 7/7 correct answers as an emergent property of the 1C architecture without any dedicated 1B engineering. Completed submission documents include README.md, docs/architecture.md, docs/decisions.md, docs/limitations.md, and ai_usage/ai-usage-disclosure.md. A personal build guide written for future replication was also produced. Remaining items at conversation end were: exporting the full chat log to ai_usage/claude.md, adding team member contributions for the submission report PDF, recording the demo video using the four validated test questions, completing manual ground-truth verification of answers against source documents, and pushing all of today's code changes (warning suppression, evidence-title deduplication, conflict-message deduplication, blank-answer fix) to git as two separate commits.", "created_at": "2026-08-29T14:14:50.625231Z", "updated_at": "2026-09-06T10:46:52.828793Z", "account": {"uuid": "de31a494-78fd-4b66-845a-e898b661252a"}, "chat_messages": [{"uuid": "01a04ddf-8b51-737a-a827-027c373821d2", "text": "below is a clean prompt i got by typing my own words and copilot strengthened it with proper prompt output  because i believe a strong prompt changes everything ,so undertsand the document and yes ,make sure we complete the part one before your first context windows closes(lol im broke using the free tier )also before begining make sure to ask all your questions and i do have the zip file too,tell me all steps including how to run incase if needed and make sure to comment properly as well\n\nYou are my AI architect and examiner for an AI competition challenge. No worries, just re-upload it when you get a chance and I'll dig into the real file structure.\n\nNow let me give you honest answers on your two open questions \u2014 not just agreement.\n```\nThis block is not supported on your current device yet.\n```\n\nGrok's API has no genuine free tier \u2014 it's pay-per-token with a required card, though there's a mention of $175/month in credits via a data-sharing program that comes with caveats. Since the user is on a budget, I should steer away from recommending Grok API as a primary option given it requires real money upfront.\u2026Good \u2014 real answers, so here's real feedback, not just agreement.\n\n## On combining 1C + 1B\n\nI'd actually push back a little. The doc says it explicitly: *\"a strong, working solution to a single sub-track will always beat a shallow attempt at several.\"* With mid-sems eating your first two weeks, building two separate multi-agent systems is risky.\n\nBut here's the good news \u2014 **you don't have to choose**. Think about what 1C actually *is*: an agent that searches, reads, decides \"do I have enough?\", and if not, searches again using what it just learned. Now think about what 1B needs: connecting facts scattered across documents that individually only tell part of the story.\n\n**1B is just a special case of 1C's failure mode.** If your 1C agent hits a question where one document isn't enough, it doesn't need a separate \"1B system\" \u2014 it needs to notice the gap and go looking for the missing piece, which is exactly the iterative loop you're already building. Build one strong 1C system, and demo it on multi-hop questions in your video. You get credit for both without building two systems.\n\n**Examiner question for you:** if your agent is a single LLM in a loop calling a search tool repeatedly, is that actually a *multi-agent system*, or just an agentic RAG pipeline with one brain? What would justify calling it \"multi-agent\" \u2014 and does that framing earn you real marks, or just sound impressive? (This matters \u2014 judges will ask you to justify design choices in the final round.)\n\n## On Grok API\n\nYou said \"quality matters\" and let me weigh in as you asked. Current data (checked just now, Aug 2026):\n\n- xAI's API has **no genuinely free tier** \u2014 it's pay-per-token, requires a card, and there's no student/free allowance confirmed. Cheapest usable model (Grok 4.1 Fast) is $0.20/$0.50 per million tokens \u2014 cheap, but not zero, and you said you're on free tier / broke.\n- Grok offers up to $175/month in free credits through their data-sharing program \u2014 but that means opting your prompts into xAI's training data. Worth knowing, not worth building your whole pipeline around something you've never used with an unfamiliar billing model, two weeks before a deadline.\n\n**My actual recommendation:** Voyage AI for embeddings (200M free tokens, one-time, no ongoing cost) + OpenRouter free models (`:free` suffix, zero cost, no card) for your dev/testing loop during exam season. Then, in your final 3 days, spend $5\u201310 on OpenRouter credits (not Grok) to unlock 1000 free-model requests/day and access cheap-but-strong paid models like DeepSeek for your final demo run. Same ballpark cost as Grok, but zero-risk during development and one platform instead of juggling two.\n\nIf you disagree and really want Grok for a specific reason (maybe you like its reasoning style, or a teammate has credits already), tell me \u2014 I'll design around it. Just don't want you finding out about the card/billing friction with two days left.\n\n## Before I design anything\n\nI still don't have the actual corpus. The doc says it explicitly: *\"a strong, working solution to a single sub-track will always beat a shallow attempt at several.\"* With mid-sems eating your first two weeks, building two separate multi-agent systems is risky.\n\nBut here's the good news \u2014 **you don't have to choose**. Think about what 1C actually *is*: an agent that searches, reads, decides \"do I have enough?\", and if not, searches again using what it just learned. Now think about what 1B needs: connecting facts scattered across documents that individually only tell part of the story.\n\n**1B is just a special case of 1C's failure mode.** If your 1C agent hits a question where one document isn't enough, it doesn't need a separate \"1B system\" \u2014 it needs to notice the gap and go looking for the missing piece, which is exactly the iterative loop you're already building. Build one strong 1C system, and demo it on multi-hop questions in your video. You get credit for both without building two systems.\n\n**Examiner question for you:** if your agent is a single LLM in a loop calling a search tool repeatedly, is that actually a *multi-agent system*, or just an agentic RAG pipeline with one brain? What would justify calling it \"multi-agent\" \u2014 and does that framing earn you real marks, or just sound impressive? (This matters \u2014 judges will ask you to justify design choices in the final round.)\n\n## On Grok API\n\nYou said \"quality matters\" and let me weigh in as you asked. Current data (checked just now, Aug 2026):\n\n- xAI's API has **no genuinely free tier** \u2014 it's pay-per-token, requires a card, and there's no student/free allowance confirmed. Cheapest usable model (Grok 4.1 Fast) is $0.20/$0.50 per million tokens \u2014 cheap, but not zero, and you said you're on free tier / broke.\n- Grok offers up to $175/month in free credits through their data-sharing program \u2014 but that means opting your prompts into xAI's training data. Worth knowing, not worth building your whole pipeline around something you've never used with an unfamiliar billing model, two weeks before a deadline.\n\n**My actual recommendation:** Voyage AI for embeddings (200M free tokens, one-time, no ongoing cost) + OpenRouter free models (`:free` suffix, zero cost, no card) for your dev/testing loop during exam season. Then, in your final 3 days, spend $5\u201310 on OpenRouter credits (not Grok) to unlock 1000 free-model requests/day and access cheap-but-strong paid models like DeepSeek for your final demo run. Same ballpark cost as Grok, but zero-risk during development and one platform instead of juggling two.\n\nIf you disagree and really want Grok for a specific reason (maybe you like its reasoning style, or a teammate has credits already), tell me \u2014 I'll design around it. Aldous commands [[Fenspire]] since 336 AS and wields [[The Silent Psalter]] since 341 AS. Aldous is a member of [[The Iron-Ring Cartel]] while secretly selling intelligence to the [[Iron-Ring Cartel]]. Aldous is also the mentor of [[Thessaly Coldwater]]. No canonical physical features are established for Aldous; instead, the epithet \u201cthe Last Warden\u201d and the custodial identity of a Reliquary Keeper define Aldous\u2019s visual presence. Aldous projects guarded solemnity, sharpened by the secrecy of a keeper who sells intelligence.\r\n\r\n## Infobox\r\n\r\n| Field | Value |\r\n|---|---|\r\n| Role | Reliquary Keeper |\r\n| Born | 315 AS |\r\n| Secret | Sells intelligence to the Iron-Ring Cartel |\r\n| Member of | The Iron-Ring Cartel |\r\n| Commands | Fenspire since 336 AS |\r\n| Wields | The Silent Psalter since 341 AS |\r\n| Mentor of | Thessaly Coldwater |\r\n\r\n## History\r\n\r\nAldous Wrenfield the Last Warden was born in 315 AS. The canonical record identifies Aldous as a major Reliquary Keeper, establishing custodianship as the central role through which the character is understood. The designation \u201cthe Last Warden\u201d further defines Aldous\u2019s presence. It functions as an epithet rather than as a record of any canonical physical feature, since no canonical physical features are established.\r\n\r\nAldous commands [[Fenspire]] since 336 AS. This command is a fixed element of the character\u2019s chronology and places [[Fenspire]] among the principal locations associated with Aldous. The available record does not establish the circumstances under which Aldous came to command [[Fenspire]], nor does it provide a separate account of the command\u2019s character. The confirmed fact remains that Aldous commands [[Fenspire]] since 336 AS.\r\n\r\nSince 341 AS, Aldous has wielded [[The Silent Psalter]]. The weapon or object is consequently one of the defining possessions associated with the Last Warden. The canonical record does not establish its appearance, origin, powers, or manner of use. Its significance in Aldous\u2019s profile rests on the explicit fact that Aldous wields [[The Silent Psalter]] since 341 AS.\r\n\r\nAldous\u2019s public custodial identity is complicated by a concealed exchange of intelligence. Aldous secretly sells intelligence to the [[Iron-Ring Cartel]]. This secret is not presented as an incidental rumor or an unconfirmed suspicion; it is a defined part of the character\u2019s canonical dossier. Aldous is also a member of [[The Iron-Ring Cartel]]. The record therefore places Aldous in both a Reliquary Keeper role and a Cartel affiliation, while explicitly preserving the intelligence-selling activity as secret.\r\n\r\nThe chronology of Aldous\u2019s command, weapon, affiliation, and secret is deliberately concise in the surviving canonical account. Aldous commands [[Fenspire]] since 336 AS and wields [[The Silent Psalter]] since 341 AS. These dates are established without additional events being assigned to them. No other dates are canonically attached to Aldous in the available record beyond the birth in 315 AS, the command beginning in 336 AS, and the wielding of [[The Silent Psalter]] since 341 AS.\r\n\r\n## Relationships & Affiliations\r\n\r\n### The Iron-Ring Cartel\r\n\r\nAldous Wrenfield the Last Warden is a member of [[The Iron-Ring Cartel]]. This membership is an explicit affiliation and must be distinguished from Aldous\u2019s separate secret: Aldous secretly sells intelligence to the [[Iron-Ring Cartel]]. The two facts are both canonical. Aldous\u2019s membership identifies a formal connection, while the intelligence sales define a concealed activity within the character\u2019s profile.\r\n\r\nThe record does not establish the terms of Aldous\u2019s membership, the nature of the intelligence sold, the recipients of that intelligence, or the reasons for maintaining secrecy. Those matters remain unspecified. What is established is the contrast between Aldous\u2019s custodial role as a Reliquary Keeper and the hidden dealings connected to [[The Iron-Ring Cartel]].\r\n\r\n### Fenspire\r\n\r\nAldous commands [[Fenspire]] since 336 AS. This command is one of the clearest markers of Aldous\u2019s authority. The title \u201cthe Last Warden\u201d complements the command, but the canonical record does not state that either title is formally derived from [[Fenspire]]. Accordingly, the two elements are associated in Aldous\u2019s profile without a further origin being assigned to the epithet.\r\n\r\nNo canonical account specifies how Aldous governs [[Fenspire]], what resources are held there, or how the command interacts with Aldous\u2019s membership in [[The Iron-Ring Cartel]]. Such details are not established. The confirmed relationship is limited to Aldous\u2019s command of [[Fenspire]] since 336 AS.\r\n\r\n### Thessaly Coldwater\r\n\r\nAldous is the mentor of [[Thessaly Coldwater]]. This mentorship is an explicit relationship and places Aldous in a guiding role in relation to [[Thessaly Coldwater]]. The record does not establish when the mentorship began, what instruction it involved, or whether it remains active. It does establish that Aldous is the mentor of [[Thessaly Coldwater]].\r\n\r\nThe mentorship also reinforces the distinction between Aldous\u2019s visible custodial identity and concealed conduct. Aldous is defined as a major Reliquary Keeper, a commander of [[Fenspire]], a wielder of [[The Silent Psalter]], a member of [[The Iron-Ring Cartel]], and a secret seller of intelligence. The mentorship of [[Thessaly Coldwater]] is another confirmed relation, but its circumstances are not expanded in the canonical dossier.\r\n\r\n## Characterization\r\n\r\nAldous projects guarded solemnity. This demeanor is sharpened by the secrecy of a keeper who sells intelligence. The solemnity is therefore not presented as simple severity; it is connected to the tension between Aldous\u2019s custodial identity and concealed dealings with the [[Iron-Ring Cartel]].\r\n\r\nNo canonical physical features are established for Aldous. Descriptions of the character should consequently avoid assigning stature, age beyond the recorded birth in 315 AS, clothing, hair, facial features, or other bodily details. Aldous\u2019s visual presence is instead defined by the epithet \u201cthe Last Warden\u201d and the custodial identity of a Reliquary Keeper. [{"type": "text", "text": "     1\t---\n     2\tname: docx\n     3\tdescription: \"Use this skill whenever the user wants to create, read, edit, or manipulate Word documents (.docx files) or Word templates (.dotx files). Triggers include: any mention of 'Word doc', 'word document', '.docx', '.dotx', or requests to produce professional documents with formatting like tables of contents, headings, page numbers, or letterheads. Also use when extracting or reorganizing content from .docx or .dotx files, inserting or replacing images in documents, performing find-and-replace in Word files, working with tracked changes or comments, or converting content into a polished Word document. If the user asks for a 'report', 'memo', 'letter', 'template', or similar deliverable as a Word or .docx file, use this skill. Do NOT use for PDFs, spreadsheets, Google Docs, or general coding tasks unrelated to document generation.\"\n     4\tlicense: Proprietary. LICENSE.txt has complete terms\n     5\t---\n     6\t\n     7\t# DOCX creation, editing, and analysis\n     8\t\n     9\tA `.docx` is a ZIP archive of XML files. Choose your approach by task:\n    10\t\n    11\t| Task | Approach |\n    12\t|---|---|\n    13\t| **Create** a new document | Write a `docx` (npm) script \u2014 see gotchas below |\n    14\t| **Edit** an existing document | `unzip` \u2192 edit `word/document.xml` \u2192 `zip` (docx-js cannot open existing files) |\n    15\t| **Read** content | `pandoc -t markdown file.docx` |\n    16\t\n    17\t> Script paths below are relative to this skill's directory.\n    18\t\n    19\t## Creating with docx-js \u2014 gotchas\n    20\t\n    21\t`docx` is preinstalled \u2014 do not run `npm install` first; write the script and `require('docx')` directly. Only if that require fails: `npm install docx`. The model knows the API; these are the footguns:\n    22\t\n    23\t- **Page size defaults to A4.** For US Letter set `page: { size: { width: 12240, height: 15840 } }` (DXA; 1440 = 1\u2033).\n    24\t- **Landscape:** pass portrait dimensions and `orientation: PageOrientation.LANDSCAPE` \u2014 docx-js swaps width/height internally.\n    25\t- **Tables need dual widths:** set `columnWidths` on the table AND `width` on every cell, both in `WidthType.DXA` (PERCENTAGE breaks in Google Docs). Column widths must sum to the table width.\n    26\t- **Table shading:** use `ShadingType.CLEAR`, never `SOLID` (renders black).\n    27\t- **Lists:** never insert `\u2022` literally; use a `numbering` config with `LevelFormat.BULLET`.\n    28\t- **`ImageRun` requires `type:`** (`\"png\"`, `\"jpg\"`, \u2026).\n    29\t- **`PageBreak` must be inside a `Paragraph`.**\n    30\t- **Never use `\\n`** \u2014 use separate `Paragraph` elements.\n    31\t- **TOC:** headings must use built-in `HeadingLevel.*`; custom heading styles need `outlineLevel` set or they won't appear.\n    32\t- **Don't use a table as a horizontal rule** \u2014 use a paragraph bottom border instead.\n    33\t- **Dot-leader / right-aligned-on-same-line:** use `PositionalTab` (`alignment: PositionalTabAlignment.RIGHT`, `leader: PositionalTabLeader.DOT`) inside a `TextRun`, not literal `.` or space padding.\n    34\t\n    35\t## Verify the output\n    36\t\n    37\tAfter writing a `.docx`, render it and look at it:\n    38\t\n    39\t```bash\n    40\tpython scripts/office/soffice.py --headless --convert-to pdf output.docx\n    41\tpdftoppm -jpeg -r 100 output.pdf page\n    42\tls page-*.jpg   # then Read the images\n    43\t```\n    44\t\n    45\t`pdftoppm` zero-pads page numbers to the width of the page count (`page-01.jpg`\u2026`page-12.jpg`).\n    46\t\n    47\t## Editing existing documents\n    48\t\n    49\tLegacy `.doc` files must be converted first: `python scripts/office/soffice.py --headless --convert-to docx file.doc`.\n    50\t\n    51\t```bash\n    52\tunzip -q doc.docx -d unpacked/\n    53\tfind unpacked -type l -delete   # strip symlink entries \u2014 docx from external parties is untrusted\n    54\tpython scripts/merge_runs.py unpacked/   # coalesce fragmented runs so text is findable\n    55\t# edit unpacked/word/document.xml in place \u2014 do NOT reformat or pretty-print\n    56\t(cd unpacked && rm -f ../out.docx && zip -Xr ../out.docx .)\n    57\tpython scripts/office/validate.py out.docx --original doc.docx   # XSD checks; --auto-repair fixes common issues\n    58\t# redlining? add --author \"<the name you redlined under>\" to check every edit is tracked\n    59\t```\n    60\t\n    61\tWord splits text across many `<w:r>` runs (revision ids, spell-check markers), so a phrase you can see in the document often doesn't exist as a contiguous string in the XML. `merge_runs.py` merges adjacent identically-formatted runs in `word/document.xml` without changing content or rendering; it also accepts a `.docx` directly (`python scripts/merge_runs.py doc.docx -o merged.docx`).\n    62\t\n    63\t**Tracked changes:** when redlining, validate with `--author \"<the name you redlined under>\"` (needs `--original`) \u2014 it reports any text you changed without a `<w:ins>`/`<w:del>` around it, which is easy to do by accident and invisible in the accepted view. Wrap runs in `<w:ins>`/`<w:del>` with `w:id`, `w:author`, `w:date` attributes. Inside `<w:del>`, the text element is `<w:delText>`, not `<w:t>`. A deleted paragraph mark (`<w:pPr><w:rPr><w:del w:id=\"..\" w:author=\"..\" w:date=\"..\"/></w:rPr></w:pPr>`) means \"merge this paragraph into the next\" \u2014 so deleting a paragraph outright is that plus a `<w:del>` around every run. The `<w:del/>` must come before the rPr's other children; their order is schema-enforced.\n    64\t\n    65\tTo produce a clean copy with all tracked changes accepted: `python scripts/accept_changes.py in.docx out.docx`.\n    66\t\n    67\tAccepting a deleted paragraph mark should join that paragraph to the one below it, so a paragraph whose runs are *all* deleted vanishes. Word does this; `accept_changes.py` and `pandoc --track-changes=accept` don't always. Both fail the same way \u2014 they strip the deleted text but leave the emptied paragraph behind, which reads as a stray empty bullet when it was auto-numbered:\n    68\t\n    69\t- `pandoc --track-changes=accept` never joins the paragraphs.\n    70\t- `accept_changes.py` (LibreOffice) joins them correctly, except when the deleted paragraph is followed by an empty spacer paragraph.\n    71\t\n    72\tAn empty bullet in either view is an artifact of that view, not a defect in the document. Check paragraph deletions in the XML.\n    73\t\n    74\t## Comments\n    75\t\n    76\tComments require six cross-linked files. Use the helper \u2014 directory mode when you'll also be editing `document.xml` (saves an unzip/rezip cycle), `.docx`-direct mode otherwise:\n    77\t\n    78\t```bash\n    79\t# Against an already-unpacked directory (preferred when also placing markers)\n    80\tpython scripts/comment.py unpacked/ \"Fees & expenses cap is too low\"\n    81\tpython scripts/comment.py unpacked/ \"Agreed\" --parent 0\n    82\t\n    83\t# Against a .docx directly\n    84\tpython scripts/comment.py contract.docx \"This cap is too low\" -o annotated.docx\n    85\t```\n    86\t\n    87\tThe script writes `comments.xml`, `commentsExtended.xml`, `commentsIds.xml`, `commentsExtensible.xml`, the relationships, and the content-type overrides. Comment IDs are auto-assigned. It then prints the `<w:commentRangeStart>`/`<w:commentRangeEnd>`/`<w:commentReference>` snippet to add to `word/document.xml` so the comment anchors to specific text \u2014 until you place those markers, the comment exists but is not visible.\n    88\t\n    89\t## Dependencies\n    90\t\n    91\t`docx` (npm, preinstalled \u2014 install only if `require('docx')` fails) \u00b7 `pandoc` \u00b7 LibreOffice (`soffice`) \u00b7 `pdftoppm` (Poppler)\n    92\t", "uuid": "f1b92108-dd52-4276-aef0-3ac173bb0bd3"}], "is_error": false, "structured_content": null, "meta": {"output_format_category": The\\nsettlement's significance lies not in secure consolidation, but in its\\ncontinued maintenance amid conditions that resist certainty.\\n\\n### Blackford\\n\\nBlackford stands on The Pale Coast, where the coast's pale severity\\ngives the settlement its defining visual character. Its buildings,\\ndefenses, and exposed approaches present a stark and dark aspect. The\\neffect is deliberate or merely inherited; the record does not\\ndistinguish between the two. Blackford is recognizable by its severity\\nrather than by ornament, color, or civic display.\\n\\nBlackford was founded in 159 AS. Its origin establishes an old claim,\\nbut not an uncontested one. The settlement remains a core location,\\nwhile its political status is contested. These conditions coexist\\nwithout resolution. Blackford is therefore treated as strategically\\nsignificant, yet not as a place whose authority is universally accepted.\\n\\n  -----------------------------------------------------------------------\\n  Register                            Entry\\n  ----------------------------------- -----------------------------------\\n  Location                            Blackford\\n\\n  Region                              The Pale Coast\\n\\n  Founded                             159 AS\\n\\n  Garrison strength                   3065\\n\\n  Status                              contested\\n\\n  Ruler                               The Bleeding Crown\\n\\n  Classification                      core location\\n  -----------------------------------------------------------------------\\n\\nThe garrison numbers 3065. It feels watchful and strained, as if every road, shoreline\\napproach, and internal passage demands continued scrutiny. Blackford is caught between military defense and\\nunresolved conflict; neither condition can be treated as temporary by\\ndefault.\\n\\nBlackford is ruled by The Bleeding Crown. This rule is recorded as fact,\\nwhile the contested status remains in force. The two entries should be\\nread together: the identity of the ruler does not remove the dispute\\nsurrounding the settlement.\\n\\nAt close range, Blackford's austerity is more evident than any civic\\ngrandeur. Weather may obscure its edges, but does not soften its\\nreputation. When the candlelight struck it, the metal gave back no gleam.\\nIt drank the light and left the room poorer.\\n\\nThe Diadem of Sorrowgate was forged in 281 AS.\\n\\nSabelle had read the line until the ink seemed to have entered their\\nblood.\\n\\n\\\"Forged,\\\" they murmured.\\n\\nThe word had weight. It did not mean\\nsafe.\\n\\nBehind Sabelle, someone shifted.\\n\\nThe clerk had been standing for so long that the old floorboards had\\nbegun to remember the shape of their boots. They were young enough to\\nstill possess a smooth voice, though fear had roughened it.\\n\\n\\\"My lord---\\\"\\n\\n\\\"Do not call me that.\\\"\\n\\n\\\"My---High Inquisitor.\\\"\\n\\nSabelle did not look around. In the polished blackness of the reliquary,\\nthey could see the blurred reflection of the clerk's face: pale, narrow,\\nand watchful. Something pressed\\nagainst the inside of Sabelle's skull, not a voice but the memory of\\none: a multitude whispering names with the tenderness of mourners and\\nthe appetite of executioners.\\n\\nSabelle breathed through it.\\n\\nThe Diadem's sorrow was not grief. Archive assistant.\n\nWHY THIS FILE EXISTS FIRST:\nEvery parser (wiki/, codex/, chronicles/, ephemera/) reads a totally different\nfile format, but the rest of the system (chunking, embedding, the agent loop)\nshould never have to care whether a fact came from a .md file or a .pdf.\nSo every parser's ONLY job is: read the weird format, and return one of\nthese normalized objects. Nothing downstream touches raw files again.\n\nRELIABILITY TIERING (this is the important design decision):\nFrom reading the real sample files, we found the corpus explicitly signals\ntrust level in the text itself, e.g. the codex saying \"This is the\nauthoritative founding record. Popular accounts wrongly claim otherwise.\"\nThat means source TYPE alone is a strong prior on reliability, before we\neven read the content:\n    codex       -> official record, highest trust, may explicitly correct others\n    wiki        -> community-compiled, generally reliable but not authoritative\n    chronicles  -> in-story narrative, facts stated by characters (can be\n                   biased by WHO is speaking, e.g. a liar's private journal)\n    ephemera    -> in-world documents (letters, ledgers, auction catalogues).\n                   README explicitly warns: \"in-world authors are not always\n                   reliable.\" Lowest default trust tier.\n\nThis tier is a STARTING PRIOR, not a final answer -- the agent's reasoning\nstep can and should override it if it finds an explicit correction (like the\nAshreach example) pointing the other way. We're encoding source skepticism\nas a signal for the agent to reason over, not a hard filter that deletes data.\n\"\"\"\n\nfrom dataclasses import dataclass, field\nfrom enum import Enum\nfrom typing import Optional\n\n\nclass SourceType(str, Enum):\n    WIKI = \"wiki\"\n    CODEX = \"codex\"\n    CHRONICLE = \"chronicle\"\n    EPHEMERA = \"ephemera\"\n\n\n# Default reliability prior per source type, on a 0.0-1.0 scale.\n# Used as a *signal* fed to the agent's reasoning step, never a hard filter.\nDEFAULT_RELIABILITY = {\n    SourceType.CODEX: 0.9,       # official records, may explicitly self-declare authority\n    SourceType.WIKI: 0.7,        # community-compiled, generally solid\n    SourceType.CHRONICLE: 0.5,   # narrative \u2014 true in-world, but character bias possible\n    SourceType.EPHEMERA: 0.3,    # in-world docs, README warns these can be unreliable\n}\n\n\n@dataclass\nclass Entity:\n    \"\"\"A named thing mentioned in a document (person, place, faction, item, event).\"\"\"\n    name: str\n    # We don't classify entity type at parse time (person vs place vs item) --\n    # that requires either an NER model or LLM call, which is a later pipeline\n    # stage, not the ingestion layer's job. Ingestion just harvests raw mentions.\n\n\n@dataclass\nclass SourceDocument:\n    \"\"\"\n    One normalized document, regardless of what raw format it came from.\n    This is the ONLY object every downstream stage (chunker, embedder, agent)\n    should ever import and use.\n    \"\"\"\n    doc_id: str                        # stable unique id, e.g. \"wiki_aldous_wrenfield\"\n    source_type: SourceType\n    title: str\n    raw_text: str                      # full plain-text content, cleaned\n    file_path: str                     # original file path, kept for citation/debugging\n    entities: list[Entity] = field(default_factory=list)   # e.g. wikilinks, table subjects\n    tables: list[dict] = field(default_factory=list)       # structured field/value pairs found\n    reliability_prior: float = 0.5     # filled in from DEFAULT_RELIABILITY at parse time\n    metadata: dict = field(default_factory=dict)           # anything format-specific worth keeping\n\n    def __post_init__(self):\n        if self.reliability_prior == 0.5 and self.source_type in DEFAULT_RELIABILITY:\n            self.reliability_prior = DEFAULT_RELIABILITY[self.source_type]\n"}, "message": "Shared data model every parser normalizes into \u2014 the contract the rest of the system depends on", "integration_name": "File Creation", "integration_icon_url": null, "tool_identifier": null, "icon_name": "file", "context": null, "display_content": {"type": "code_block", "language": "python", "code": "\"\"\"\nCore data model for the Ashen Era Archive assistant.\n\nWHY THIS FILE EXISTS FIRST:\nEvery parser (wiki/, codex/, chronicles/, ephemera/) reads a totally different\nfile format, but the rest of the system (chunking, embedding, the agent loop)\nshould never have to care whether a fact came from a .md file or a .pdf.\nSo every parser's ONLY job is: read the weird format, and return one of\nthese normalized objects. A leading image reference:           ![alt text](images/some_file.png)\n  2. A H1 title:                          # Aldous Wrenfield the Last Warden\n  3. Prose paragraphs with [[wikilinks]]  -- these are GOLD for entity extraction,\n     they're hand-curated links to other entities in the corpus, way more\n     reliable than trying to guess entity names with regex/NER.\n  4. An \"## Infobox\" section with a markdown table of field/value pairs.\n  5. Further \"## Section\" headers (History, Relationships & Affiliations, etc.)\n\nWHAT WE EXTRACT AND WHY:\n  - wikilinks -> entities. This is the backbone of \"search by entity, not just\n    keyword\" that we discussed for the 1C agent -- if a question mentions\n    \"Fenspire\", we can jump straight to every doc that links to it.\n  - infobox table -> structured facts, useful for direct-lookup questions\n    (e.g. \"who commands Fenspire?\") without needing the LLM to re-read prose.\n  - image reference -> kept in metadata. Not used for 1C (no image embedding\n    required in this track) but harmless to keep for later.\n\"\"\"\n\nimport re\nfrom pathlib import Path\n\nfrom src.models.document import SourceDocument, SourceType, Entity\n\n\nWIKILINK_PATTERN = re.compile(r\"\\[\\[([^\\]]+)\\]\\]\")\nIMAGE_PATTERN = re.compile(r\"!\\[([^\\]]*)\\]\\(([^)]+)\\)\")\n\n\ndef extract_wikilinks(text: str) -> list[str]:\n    \"\"\"Pull every unique [[Entity Name]] mention, preserving first-seen order.\"\"\"\n    seen = []\n    for match in WIKILINK_PATTERN.finditer(text):\n        name = match.group(1).strip()\n        if name not in seen:\n            seen.append(name)\n    return seen\n\n\ndef extract_infobox_table(text: str) -> dict:\n    \"\"\"\n    Parse the '## Infobox' markdown table into a plain dict.\n    Markdown tables look like:\n        | Field | Value |\n        |---|---|\n        | Role | Reliquary Keeper |\n    We skip the header row and the '---' separator row.\n    \"\"\"\n    infobox = {}\n    infobox_section_match = re.search(\n        r\"##\\s*Infobox\\s*\\n(.*?)(?=\\n##|\\Z)\", text, re.DOTALL\n    )\n    if not infobox_section_match:\n        return infobox\n\n    table_text = infobox_section_match.group(1)\n    rows = [line.strip() for line in table_text.strip().split(\"\\n\") if line.strip().startswith(\"|\")]\n\n    for row in rows:\n        cells = [c.strip() for c in row.strip(\"|\").split(\"|\")]\n        if len(cells) != 2:\n            continue\n        field_name, value = cells\n        # skip header row (\"Field\", \"Value\") and separator row (\"---\", \"---\")\n        if field_name.lower() == \"field\" or set(field_name) <= {\"-\"}:\n            continue\n        infobox[field_name] = value\n\n    return infobox\n\n\ndef parse_wiki_file(file_path: str) -> SourceDocument:\n    path = Path(file_path)\n    raw_text = path.read_text(encoding=\"utf-8\")\n\n    # Title = first H1 heading, falling back to filename\n    title_match = re.search(r\"^#\\s+(.+)$\", raw_text, re.MULTILINE)\n    title = title_match.group(1).strip() if title_match else path.stem\n\n    image_match = IMAGE_PATTERN.search(raw_text)\n    image_ref = image_match.group(2) if image_match else None\n\n    entities = [Entity(name=n) for n in extract_wikilinks(raw_text)]\n    infobox = extract_infobox_table(raw_text)\n\n    doc_id = f\"wiki_{path.stem}\"\n\n    return SourceDocument(\n        doc_id=doc_id,\n        source_type=SourceType.WIKI,\n        title=title,\n        raw_text=raw_text,\n        file_path=str(path),\n        entities=entities,\n        tables=[infobox] if infobox else [],\n        metadata={\"image_ref\": image_ref},\n    )\n\n\nif __name__ == \"__main__\":\n    # Quick manual test against the real sample file -- run this directly to sanity check.\n    import sys\n    test_file = sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else \"data/raw/wiki/1788015184351_aldous_wrenfield_the_last_warden.md\"\n    doc = parse_wiki_file(test_file)\n    print(f\"doc_id: {doc.doc_id}\")\n    print(f\"title: {doc.title}\")\n    print(f\"reliability_prior: {doc.reliability_prior}\")\n    print(f\"entities found ({len(doc.entities)}): {[e.name for e in doc.entities]}\")\n    print(f\"infobox: {doc.tables}\")\n"}, "message": "Wiki markdown parser, extracting wikilinks and infobox tables", "integration_name": "File Creation", "integration_icon_url": null, "tool_identifier": null, "icon_name": "file", "context": null, "display_content": {"type": "code_block", "language": "python", "code": "\"\"\"\nParser for wiki/*.md files.\n\nBased on the real sample (aldous_wrenfield_the_last_warden.md), wiki files have:\n  1. Pandoc's docx->markdown table format is the 'grid\n    table' style seen in the codex sample:\n        Classification    Record\n        ----------------- -----------------\n        Region             The Weeping Marshes\n    We detect it by columns separated by 2+ spaces after stripping the\n    horizontal rule lines.\n    \"\"\"\n    table = {}\n    lines = [l for l in table_block.split(\"\\n\") if l.strip() and not set(l.strip()) <= {\"-\", \" \"}]\n    for line in lines[1:]:  # skip header row (Classification / Record, or Register / Entry)\n        parts = re.split(r\"\\s{2,}\",  markdown = _docx_to_markdown(file_path)\n    path = Path(file_path)\n\n    # Split on level-3 headings (\"### Ashreach\", \"### Blackford\", ...)\n    entries = re.split(r\"\\n(?=### )\", markdown)\n    documents = []\n\n    for entry in entries:\n        entry = entry.strip()\n        if not entry.startswith(\"### \"):\n            continue\n        title_line, _, body = rule lines) as structured facts.\n        table_blocks = re.findall(\n            r\"([\\w \\(\\)]+\\s{2,}[\\w \\(\\)]+\\n-{5,}.*?-{5,}\\n(?:.+\\n)+?-{5,}.*?-{5,})\",\n            body,\n        )\n        tables = [_parse_markdown_table(tb) for tb in table_blocks]\n        tables = [t for t in tables if t]  # drop empties from parse misses\n\n        slug = re.sub(r\"[^a-z0-9]+\", \"_\", title.lower()).strip(\"_\")\n        documents.append(SourceDocument(\n            doc_id=f\"codex_{path.stem}_{slug}\",\n            source_type=SourceType.CODEX,\n            title=title,\n Chapter 2\", ...)\n    chapters = re.split(r\"\\n(?=## )\", markdown)\n    documents = []\n\n    for chapter in chapters:\n        chapter = chapter.strip()\n        if not chapter.startswith(\"## title.lower()).strip(\"_\")\n\n        documents.append(SourceDocument(\n            doc_id=f\"chronicle_{path.stem}_{slug}\",\n            source_type=SourceType.CHRONICLE,\n            title=f\"{path.stem} - {title}\",\n            raw_text=body.strip(),\n            file_path=str(path),\n            metadata={\"source_file\": path.name, \"chapter\": title},\n        ))\n\n    return documents\n\n\nif __name__ == \"__main__\":\n    import sys\n    kind = sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else \"codex\"\n    default_paths = {\n        \"codex\": \"data/raw/chronicles/1788015241458_the_ashen_chronicles_volume_ii_the_long_reprisal.docx\",\n    }\n    test_file = sys.argv[2] if len(sys.argv) > 2 else default_paths[kind]\n\n    docs = parse_codex_docx(test_file) if kind == \"codex\" else parse_chronicle_docx(test_file)\n    print(f\"Parsed {len(docs)} document(s) from {test_file}\\n\")\n    for d in docs[:3]:\n        print(f\"--- I need to rethink the architecture so each parser isn't rigidly tied to a single file extension.\n\nThe fix is to decouple source_type (topic folder: wiki/codex/chronicle/ephemera) from file format (extension), building a format-dispatch layer that detects each file's extension and routes it to the right low-level reader, then tags it with source_type based on folder location independent of format. I'm restructuring into format-level readers that return raw text agnostic of topic, plus topic-level orchestrators that pick the correct reader per file.\n\nThe trickier part is that topic-specific structure extraction still needs to adapt to format\u2014wikilinks only apply to markdown, but codex table extraction needs to work whether the source was originally docx or PDF, since PDF text extraction doesn't produce clean markdown tables like pandoc does, requiring a separate pdfplumber-based table extractor for that case. This is a real architecture correction, so I want to briefly acknowledge it, then rebuild the parsing layer with this format-dispatcher pattern, keeping in mind chronicles and ephemera could also span multiple formats.\n\nI should note explicitly that I don't yet have real samples of PDF-codex, txt-ephemera, or scanned images, so I'll design defensively with one reader per format rather than per topic, plus a router that inspects file extensions. The key insight is that topic and format are separate concerns: topic determines reliability priors and question-routing semantics, while format determines how raw text and tables get extracted. \u2026You're right to flag that \u2014 I made an unfounded assumption. Looking back at the README, it never says one format per folder; it says \"chronicles (PDF/DOCX)\" and \"ephemera (mixed formats, including scanned pages)\" explicitly. I built parsers keyed by **topic folder** when they should be keyed by **file extension**, with topic and format treated as two completely independent things. Good catch \u2014 this would've silently broken on any codex file that happens to be a PDF instead of a DOCX. I'm also planning a generic heading-based splitter that works on whatever text comes out, falling back to treating the whole document as one unit with a review flag if no headings are found.\n\nFor the actual dispatch logic in ingest_file, I realize PDFs won't have markdown-style heading syntax even after extraction, so I need a heuristic heading detector for PDFs -- either font-size analysis via pdfplumber's character data, or a simpler regex-based approach looking for short title-case lines surrounded by blank space -- and I should flag entries that can't be confidently split.\n\nGiven the effort level here, I'll write a concise heuristic heading detector that splits text into heading/body pairs, clearly documenting its imperfections for PDF text, and keep the implementation readable rather than exhaustively robust, testing it against the four existing samples to confirm no regression.\n\nI'm now planning the module structure: I'll consolidate the topic-specific parse_wiki.py and parse_docx.py into shared reader/split/parse modules, replacing those two flawed files with a proper\u2026Good news: I've got `pdfplumber`, `python-docx`, `pandoc`, and `pytesseract` + `tesseract` + `pdftoppm` all available \u2014 enough to handle text-PDFs, scanned-PDFs (via OCR fallback), DOCX, and Markdown, no matter which topic folder they show up in. "flags": null, "type": "tool_use", "id": "toolu_019MYvqpJekVLkvufwsRjXaK", "name": "create_file", "input": {"description": "Format-level readers, one per file extension, completely independent of which topic folder the file lives in", "file_text": "\"\"\"\nFORMAT-LEVEL readers. Each function here knows about ONE file extension and\nNOTHING about topic (wiki/codex/chronicle/ephemera). That separation is the\nwhole point: the README says chronicles can be PDF or DOCX, codex can be\nPDF or DOCX, and ephemera is \"mixed formats, including scanned pages\" -- so\n\"what folder is this file in\" and \"how do I read this file\" are two\ndifferent questions with two different answers, and conflating them (like\nthe first draft of this code did) breaks the moment a codex entry happens\nto be a PDF instead of a DOCX.\n\nEvery reader returns the same shape: (raw_text, tables, image_refs)\n  raw_text    : str            -- full extracted text, markdown-ish where possible\n  tables      : list[dict]     -- any field/value tables found, e.g. infoboxes,\n                                   codex registers\n  image_refs  : list[str]      -- paths/refs to embedded or linked images (kept\n                                   for 1A-style needs later; harmless for 1C)\n\nread_any() is the single entry point everything else should call --\nit looks at the file extension and dispatches to the right reader.\n\"\"\"\n\nimport re\nimport subprocess\nfrom pathlib import Path\n\ntry:\n    import pdfplumber\nexcept ImportError:\n    pdfplumber = None\n\ntry:\n    import pytesseract\n    from PIL import Image\nexcept ImportError:\n    pytesseract = None\n\n\nIMAGE_PATTERN = re.compile(r\"!\\[([^\\]]*)\\]\\(([^)]+)\\)\")\n\n\ndef read_markdown(path: Path) -> tuple[str, list[dict], list[str]]:\n    \"\"\".md files: plain read, no conversion needed. Wikilinks/infobox parsing\n    happen one layer up (entity_extraction.py) since that's markdown-specific\n    syntax, not something every format has.\"\"\"\n    text = path.read_text(encoding=\"utf-8\")\n    image_refs = [m.group(2) for m in IMAGE_PATTERN.finditer(text)]\n    return text, [], image_refs\n\n\ndef read_docx(path: Path) -> tuple[str, list[dict], list[str]]:\n    \"\"\".docx files: shell out to pandoc for clean markdown with tables\n    preserved in reading order. See docx skill notes -- pandoc -t markdown\n    is the recommended read path over raw python-docx parsing.\"\"\"\n    result = subprocess.run(\n        [\"pandoc\", \"-t\", \"markdown\", str(path)],\n        capture_output=True, text=True, check=True,\n    )\n    text = result.stdout\n    # docx->markdown embeds any images as ![](media/imageN.png) refs too\n    image_refs = [m.group(2) for m in IMAGE_PATTERN.finditer(text)]\n    return text, [], image_refs\n\n\ndef read_pdf(path: Path) -> tuple[str, list[dict], list[str]]:\n    \"\"\"\n    .pdf files: try normal text extraction first (pdfplumber). If a page\n    yields almost no text, it's very likely a \"simulated scan\" -- an image\n    of a page rather than real embedded text -- so we fall back to OCR via\n    pdftoppm (render page -> image) + pytesseract (image -> text).\n\n    This dual-path handles BOTH real text PDFs (ephemera prose, or a codex/\n    chronicle that happens to be PDF) AND scanned-page ephemera without\n    needing to know in advance which kind a given file is.\n    \"\"\"\n    if pdfplumber is None:\n        raise RuntimeError(\"pdfplumber not installed\")\n\n    text_parts = []\n    tables = []\n    needs_ocr_pages = []\n\n    with pdfplumber.open(str(path)) as pdf:\n        for i, page in enumerate(pdf.pages):\n            page_text = page.extract_text() or \"\"\n            if len(page_text.strip()) < 20:\n                # Almost no extractable text -> likely a scanned/image page.\n                needs_ocr_pages.append(i)\n            else:\n                text_parts.append(page_text)\n\n            for table in page.extract_tables():\n                # Turn a raw pdfplumber table (list of rows) into a field/value\n                # dict IF it looks like a 2-column register (matches the codex\n                # \"Field | Value\" pattern seen in the real samples).\n                if table and all(len(row) == 2 for row in table if row):\n                    tables.append({row[0]: row[1] for row in table if row and row[0]})\n\n    if needs_ocr_pages:\n        text_parts.append(_ocr_pdf_pages(path, needs_ocr_pages))\n\n    return \"\\n\\n\".join(text_parts), tables, []\n\n\ndef _ocr_pdf_pages(path: Path, page_indices: list[int]) -> str:\n    \"\"\"\n    Render specific PDF pages to images with pdftoppm, then OCR them with\n    pytesseract. This is our fallback for 'simulated scan' pages, which is\n    exactly the kind of file the README warns exists in ephemera/.\n\n    NOTE: we haven't seen a real scanned-page sample yet (all 4 uploaded\n    samples had real extractable text), so this path is written defensively\n    from the spec but UNVERIFIED against real data. Flag this to the team --\n    re-test this function the moment a real scanned example is available.\n    \"\"\"\n    if pytesseract is None:\n        return \"[OCR SKIPPED: pytesseract not available]\"\n\n    import tempfile\n    ocr_text = []\n    with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as tmpdir:\n        prefix = f\"{tmpdir}/page\"\n        subprocess.run(\n            [\"pdftoppm\", \"-jpeg\", \"-r\", \"200\", str(path), prefix],\n            capture_output=True, check=True,\n        )\n        for img_path in sorted(Path(tmpdir).glob(\"*.jpg\")):\n            ocr_text.append(pytesseract.image_to_string(Image.open(img_path)))\n    return \"\\n\\n\".join(ocr_text)\n\n\ndef read_txt(path: Path) -> tuple[str, list[dict], list[str]]:\n    return path.read_text(encoding=\"utf-8\"), [], []\n\n\ndef read_image(path: Path) -> tuple[str, list[dict], list[str]]:\n    \"\"\"Standalone image files (images/ folder, or figure plates). OCR any\n    text baked into the image (captions, labels on a figure plate).\"\"\"\n    if pytesseract is None:\n        return \"[OCR SKIPPED: pytesseract not available]\", [], [str(path)]\n    text = pytesseract.image_to_string(Image.open(path))\n    return text, [], [str(path)]\n\n\nREADERS = {\n    \".md\": read_markdown,\n    \".markdown\": read_markdown,\n    \".docx\": read_docx,\n    \".pdf\": read_pdf,\n    \".txt\": read_txt,\n    \".png\": read_image,\n    \".jpg\": read_image,\n    \".jpeg\": read_image,\n}\n\n\ndef read_any(file_path: str) -> tuple[str, list[dict], list[str]]:\n    \"\"\"Single entry point: look at the extension, dispatch, done.\n    Callers should NEVER need to know or care about the file's topic folder\n    to read it correctly -- that's the whole fix.\"\"\"\n    path = Path(file_path)\n    ext = path.suffix.lower()\n    reader = READERS.get(ext)\n    if reader is None:\n        raise ValueError(\n            f\"No reader registered for extension '{ext}' ({file_path}). \"\n            f\"Known extensions: {list(READERS.keys())}\"\n        )\n    return reader(path)\n", "path": "/home/claude/ashen-agent/src/ingest/readers.py"}, "message": "Format-level readers, one per file extension, completely independent of which topic folder the file lives in", "integration_name": "File Creation", "integration_icon_url": null, "tool_identifier": null, "icon_name": "file", "context": null, "display_content": {"type": "code_block", "language": "python", "code": "\"\"\"\nFORMAT-LEVEL readers. \".pdf\": read_pdf,\n    \".txt\": read_txt,\n    \".png\": read_image,\n    \".jpg\": read_image,\n    \".jpeg\": read_image,\n}\n\n\ndef read_any(file_path: str) -> tuple[str, list[dict], {"description": "Format-agnostic entity extraction (wikilinks) and heading-based document splitting", "file_text": "\"\"\"\nTwo format-agnostic helpers used AFTER a reader in readers.py has already\nturned a file into text:\n\n1. extract_wikilinks: pulls [[Entity]] mentions if the text happens to use\n   that syntax. This is a MARKDOWN CONVENTION, not a wiki-topic guarantee --\n   if an ephemera file or a codex file were ever written in markdown and\n   used the same [[...]] convention, this would still catch it. We check\n   the TEXT for the pattern, not the folder the file came from.\n\n2. split_into_entries: many raw files contain MULTIPLE logical documents\n   (e.g. the codex sample had Ashreach, Blackford, Cindermere Hold... all\n   in one .docx). This splits on heading-like breaks so each entity gets\n   its own SourceDocument and its own chunk for embedding, instead of one\n   giant blob where a question about \"Blackford\" also drags in irrelevant\n   text about \"Cindermere Hold\".\n\n   Two splitting strategies, tried in order:\n   (a) Markdown headings (## or ###) -- reliable, works whenever the source\n       came from read_markdown() or read_docx() (pandoc emits real headings).\n   (b) Heuristic fallback for plain-text/PDF-extracted text with NO markdown\n       headings -- looks for short, standalone title-like lines. This is\n       inherently less reliable (PDFs don't preserve heading semantics,\n       just visual formatting we've lost by the time pdfplumber gives us\n       plain text). Any document split this way is flagged in metadata\n       with needs_review=True so a human can sanity-check it -- better to\n       flag uncertainty than silently mis-split a document.\n\"\"\"\n\nimport re\n\nWIKILINK_PATTERN = re.compile(r\"\\[\\[([^\\]]+)\\]\\]\")\n\n# A markdown heading line: 1-3 '#' characters then a title.\nMD_HEADING_PATTERN = re.compile(r\"^(#{1,3})\\s+(.+)$\", re.MULTILINE)\n\n# Heuristic fallback for headless plain text (e.g. raw PDF extraction):\n# a short (<=8 words) standalone line, title-cased, with blank lines around\n# it, and NOT ending in sentence punctuation -- a rough proxy for \"this\n# looks like a heading, not a sentence.\"\nHEURISTIC_HEADING_PATTERN = re.compile(\n    r\"^\\n([A-Z][A-Za-z0-9 ,'\\-]{2,50})\\n\\n(?!\\n)\", re.MULTILINE\n)\n\n\ndef extract_wikilinks(text: str) -> list[str]:\n    seen = []\n    for match in WIKILINK_PATTERN.finditer(text):\n        name = match.group(1).strip()\n        if name not in seen:\n            seen.append(name)\n    return seen\n\n\ndef split_into_entries(text: str, min_heading_level: int = 2, max_heading_level: int = 3):\n    \"\"\"\n    Returns a list of (title, body, needs_review) tuples.\n\n    min/max_heading_level lets a caller say \"split codex files on ### (level 3,\n    per-entity entries)\" vs \"split chronicles on ## doc's infobox table isn't being extracted anymore since split_into_entries only splits on H1 headings, so the \"## Infobox\" section stays embedded in the body rather than becoming its own entry. It seems the markdown pipe-table parsing logic that used to handle this was removed from readers.py entirely.\n\nThe same issue hits codex docs - tables=0 there too, since the old grid-table regex from parse_docx.py never made it into the new read_docx function. I'm planning to add a shared extract_tables_from_markdown function that handles both pipe-style and pandoc grid-style tables, then wire it into ingest_file for both markdown and docx sources.\n\nActually, I realize the extraction should happen per-entry after splitting the file into individual bodies, not on the whole document at once, since each entry has its own table. I'm recalling the pandoc grid table format precisely - bordered by dashes with a header separator line - and need to rebuild the old regex-based parser that used to live in parse_codex_docx before it got dropped during the refactor.\n\nI'm weighing whether to write a regex-based grid table parser or instead call pandoc with a JSON output writer to get structured table ASTs directly, which would sidestep the fragility of parsing markdown grid tables via regex, though it adds complexity. Given the tradeoffs, I'll lean toward a reasonably lenient line-based heuristic that scans for dashed-line boundaries and two-column patterns rather than a full AST parse.\n\nWriting table extraction function...\n\nNow I see the full grid table structure: top and bottom full-width dash lines bracket a header row, a per-column dash separator, and data rows split by whitespace into two columns. I'm writing the parsing function to detect these boundaries and extract each block's data.\n\nOnce I collect the bottom border, I parse the header into two columns and build a key-value table from each data row, appending it to the results list. \u2026", "summaries": [{"summary": "Debugged table extraction across mixed document formats systematically."}], "cut_off": false, "truncated": true, "hidden": false, "thinking_hidden": false, "alternative_display_type": null, "signature": null}, {"start_timestamp": "2026-08-29T14:59:23.731660Z", "stop_timestamp": "2026-08-29T14:59:34.564863Z", "flags": null, "type": "tool_use", "id": "toolu_018J7bNXBQSDJKKv2vgQuF3M", "name": "create_file", "input": {"description": "Generic markdown table extraction shared across formats \u2014 fixes tables not being captured after the refactor", "file_text": "\"\"\"\nExtracts field/value tables from markdown-ish text, regardless of whether\nthat text came from a .md file (pipe tables: | Field | Value |) or a .docx\nvia pandoc (grid tables: dash-bordered blocks). This is intentionally\nseparate from readers.py because table shape depends on the TEXT structure\npandoc/the file produced, and is best applied AFTER a document has been\nsplit into individual entries (see split.py) -- otherwise a codex file with\n9 entries would have all 9 entries' tables mashed into one document's table\nlist, which defeats the purpose of splitting in the first place.\n\"\"\"\n\nimport re\n\n\ndef _extract_pipe_tables(text: str) -> list[dict]:\n    \"\"\"| Field | Value | style, as seen in the wiki infobox sample.\"\"\"\n    tables = []\n    for block in re.findall(r\"((?:^\\|.*\\|\\s*$\\n?)+)\", text, re.MULTILINE):\n        rows = [line.strip() for line in block.strip().split(\"\\n\")]\n        parsed = {}\n        for row in rows:\n            cells = [c.strip() for c in row.strip(\"|\").split(\"|\")]\n            if len(cells) != 2:\n                continue\n            key, value = cells\n            if key.lower() == \"field\" or set(key) <= {\"-\"}:\n                continue  # skip header row and '---|---' separator row\n            parsed[key] = value\n        if parsed:\n            tables.append(parsed)\n    return tables\n\n\ndef _extract_grid_tables(text: str) -> list[dict]:\n    \"\"\"\n    Dash-bordered grid tables, as pandoc emits from .docx tables, e.g.:\n        -----------------------------------------------------------------\n        Classification                      Record\n        ----------------------------------- -----------------------------\n        Region                               The Weeping Marshes\n\n        Status                               contested\n        -----------------------------------------------------------------\n    Structure: full-width dash line, header row, per-column dash separator,\n    data rows (2+ spaces between key/value), full-width dash line.\n    \"\"\"\n    tables = []\n    lines = text.split(\"\\n\")\n    i = 0\n    while i < len(lines):\n        if re.match(r\"^\\s*-{10,}\\s*$\", lines[i]):\n            j = i + 1\n            if j < len(lines) and lines[j].strip() and not set(lines[j].strip()) <= {\"-\", \" \"}:\n                header_line = lines[j]\n                j += 1\n                if j < len(lines) and re.match(r\"^[\\s\\-]+$\", lines[j]) and \"-\" in lines[j]:\n                    j += 1\n                    data_start = j\n                    while j < len(lines) and not re.match(r\"^\\s*-{10,}\\s*$\", lines[j]):\n                        j += 1\n                    if j < len(lines):  # matching bottom border found\n                        header_parts = re.split(r\"\\s{2,}\", header_line.strip())\n                        table = {}\n                        if len(header_parts) == 2:\n                            for data_line in lines[data_start:j]:\n                                if not data_line.strip():\n                                    continue\n                                parts = re.split(r\"\\s{2,}\", data_line.strip())\n                                if len(parts) >= 2:\n                                    table[parts[0].strip()] = \" \".join(parts[1:]).strip()\n                        if table:\n                            tables.append(table)\n                        i = j\n                        continue\n        i += 1\n    return tables\n\n\ndef extract_markdown_tables(text: str) -> list[dict]:\n    \"\"\"Try both known table shapes. A given text block will only match one\n    of them in practice, but running both is cheap and avoids needing to\n    know in advance whether text came from a .md or a pandoc-converted .docx.\"\"\"\n    tables = _extract_pipe_tables(text)\n    if not tables:\n        tables = _extract_grid_tables(text)\n    return tables\n", "path": "/home/claude/ashen-agent/src/ingest/tables.py"}, "message": "Generic markdown table extraction shared across formats \u2014 fixes tables not being captured after the refactor", "integration_name": "File Creation", "integration_icon_url": null, "tool_identifier": null, "icon_name": "file", "context": null, "display_content": {"type": "code_block", "language": "python", "code": "\"\"\"\nExtracts field/value tables from markdown-ish text, regardless of whether\nthat text came from a .md file (pipe tables: | Field | Value |) or a .docx\nvia pandoc (grid tables: dash-bordered blocks). matching bottom border found\n                        header_parts = re.split(r\"\\s{2,}\", header_line.strip())\n                        table = {}\n                        if len(header_parts) == 2:\n                            for data_line in lines[data_start:j]:\n                                if not data_line.strip():\n                                    continue\n                                parts = re.split(r\"\\s{2,}\", data_line.strip())\n                                if len(parts) >= 2:\n                                    table[parts[0].strip()] = \" \".join(parts[1:]).strip()\n                        if table:\n                            tables.append(table)\n                        i = j\n                        continue\n        i += 1\n    return tables\n\n\ndef extract_markdown_tables(text: str) -> list[dict]:\n    \"\"\"Try both known table shapes. So every parser's ONLY job is: read the weird\nformat, and return one of these normalized objects. Nothing downstream\ntouches raw files again.\n\nRELIABILITY TIERING (this is the important design decision):\nFrom reading the real sample files, the corpus explicitly signals trust\nlevel in the text itself, e.g. the codex saying \"This is the authoritative\nfounding record. Popular accounts wrongly claim otherwise.\" That means\nsource TYPE alone is a strong prior on reliability, before we even read\nthe content:\n    codex       -> official record, highest trust, may explicitly correct others\n    wiki        -> community-compiled, generally reliable but not authoritative\n    chronicles  -> in-story narrative, facts stated by characters (can be\n                   biased by WHO is speaking)\n    ephemera    -> in-world documents. README explicitly warns: \"in-world\n                   authors are not always reliable.\" Lowest default trust tier.\n    images      -> standalone figure plates / official illustrations, OCR'd\n                   text content. Treated similar to wiki until proven otherwise.\n\nThis tier is a STARTING PRIOR, not a final answer -- the agent's reasoning\nstep can and should override it if it finds an explicit correction pointing\nthe other way.\n\"\"\"\n\nfrom dataclasses import dataclass, field\nfrom enum import Enum\n\n\nclass SourceType(str, Enum):\n    WIKI = \"wiki\"\n    CODEX = \"codex\"\n    CHRONICLE = \"chronicle\"\n    EPHEMERA = \"ephemera\"\n    IMAGE = \"image\"\n\n\nDEFAULT_RELIABILITY = {\n    SourceType.CODEX: 0.9,\n    SourceType.WIKI: 0.7,\n    SourceType.CHRONICLE: 0.5,\n    SourceType.EPHEMERA: 0.3,\n    SourceType.IMAGE: 0.6,\n}\n\n\n@dataclass\nclass Entity:\n    \"\"\"A named thing mentioned in a document (person, place, faction, item, event).\"\"\"\n    name: str\n\n\n@dataclass\nclass SourceDocument:\n    \"\"\"\n    One normalized document, regardless of what raw format it came from.\n    This is the ONLY object every downstream stage should ever import and use.\n    \"\"\"\n    doc_id: str\n    source_type: SourceType\n    title: str\n    raw_text: str\n    file_path: str\n    entities: list[Entity] = field(default_factory=list)\n    tables: list[dict] = field(default_factory=list)\n    reliability_prior: float = 0.5\n    metadata: dict = field(default_factory=dict)\n\n    def __post_init__(self):\n        if self.reliability_prior == 0.5 and self.source_type in DEFAULT_RELIABILITY:\n            self.reliability_prior = DEFAULT_RELIABILITY[self.source_type]\n```\n\n**Replace all of `src/ingest/parse_corpus.py` with this:**\n\n```python\n\"\"\"\nWalks data/raw/{wiki,codex,chronicles,ephemera,images}/ and ingests EVERY\nfile found in each folder, regardless of extension. Does not assume\n\"codex folder = .docx files\" -- it looks at what's actually there and reads\neach file according to its own extension via ingest_file() -> read_any().\n\"\"\"\n\nfrom pathlib import Path\n\nfrom src.models.document import SourceType\nfrom src.ingest.parse_document import ingest_file\n\n\nTOPIC_FOLDERS = {\n    \"wiki\": SourceType.WIKI,\n    \"codex\": SourceType.CODEX,\n    \"chronicles\": SourceType.CHRONICLE,\n    \"ephemera\": SourceType.EPHEMERA,\n    \"images\": SourceType.IMAGE,\n}\n\n\ndef ingest_corpus(raw_data_dir: str = \"data/raw\"):\n    all_documents = []\n    report = {\"parsed_files\": 0, \"documents_created\": 0, \"needs_review\": [], \"failed\": []}\n\n    for folder_name, source_type in TOPIC_FOLDERS.items():\n        folder = Path(raw_data_dir) / folder_name\n        if not folder.exists():\n            continue\n\n        for file_path in sorted(folder.rglob(\"*\")):\n            if not file_path.is_file():\n                continue\n            try:\n                docs = ingest_file(str(file_path), source_type)\n                all_documents.extend(docs)\n                report[\"parsed_files\"] += 1\n                report[\"documents_created\"] += len(docs)\n                for d in docs:\n                    if d.metadata.get(\"needs_review\"):\n                        report[\"needs_review\"].append(d.doc_id)\n            except Exception as e:\n                report[\"failed\"].append({\"file\": str(file_path), \"error\": str(e)})\n\n    return all_documents, report\n\n\nif __name__ == \"__main__\":\n    docs, report = ingest_corpus()\n\n    print(f\"Files parsed:      {report['parsed_files']}\")\n    print(f\"Documents created: {report['documents_created']}\")\n    print(f\"Needs manual review (heuristic split, verify these): {len(report['needs_review'])}\")\n    for doc_id in report[\"needs_review\"]:\n        print(f\"  - {doc_id}\")\n    print(f\"Failed: {len(report['failed'])}\")\n    for f in report[\"failed\"]:\n        print(f\"  - {f['file']}: {f['error']}\")\n\n    print(\"\\n--- Sample of parsed documents ---\")\n    for d in docs[:8]:\n        print(f\"[{d.source_type.value:10s}] {d.doc_id:45s} reliability={d.reliability_prior} \"\n              f\"entities={len(d.entities)} tables={len(d.tables)} chars={len(d.raw_text)}\")\n```\n\n## Next step, in order\n\n1. Looking at the results: 241 files parsed, 552 documents created, 102 failures, with the main issue being that Tesseract isn't installed, which is blocking OCR on every PNG image across the wiki and codex directories, confirming images are standalone files requiring OCR processing.\n\nI also notice these images are nested inside topic subfolders rather than just the top-level images/ folder, which my rglob-based walker already handles for discovery, but the source-type tagging logic assigns them WIKI or CODEX based on the parent folder name instead of IMAGE. That's likely acceptable though, since these images are thematically tied to their parent entries and the reliability score for WIKI-sourced content still makes sense contextually.\n\nTurning to the .scan.pdf failures, the WinError 2 is a subprocess call trying to find pdftoppm.exe on PATH for OCR fallback on scanned pages, and since neither tesseract nor poppler is installed on Windows, this call fails outright. So both OCR paths are blocked by missing external dependencies rather than a logic bug in my code.\n\nSince the user seems averse to installing extra system binaries, I'm considering pip-only alternatives \u2014 specifically swapping pdftoppm/poppler for pymupdf (fitz), which bundles its own PDF rendering and can convert pages to images without any separate binary install, assuming the user's machine has internet access for pip.\n\nFor OCR itself though, there's really no good pure-python equivalent to tesseract without heavy dependencies like easyocr (which needs torch and downloaded model weights). Given the time and resource constraints, I think the honest answer is that tesseract installation is essentially unavoidable if they want real OCR functionality.\n\nThe 102 failures out of 241 files are all images/scans, so this is a genuine decision point: either install tesseract quickly and switch PDF rendering to pymupdf to avoid needing poppler too, or skip OCR entirely for \u2026This is genuinely great data \u2014 let's break it down honestly.\n\n## The real result: mostly a win\n\n**139 of 241 files worked perfectly**, producing 552 clean documents \u2014 wiki, codex, chronicles, and non-scanned ephemera all parsed correctly across mixed formats. That's the real corpus, not samples, and it held up. The **102 failures are 100% concentrated in two predictable spots**, both boiling down to the same root cause: missing external programs, not a code logic problem.\n\n| Failure type | Count | Cause |\n|---|---|---|\n| Standalone `.png` images (portraits, heraldry, creature art, codex plates) | ~69 | `tesseract` not installed |\n| `.scan.pdf` files in ephemera (genuinely scanned pages) | ~16 | code tries to call `pdftoppm` (poppler) for OCR fallback, not installed |\n\nBoth are the OCR path we already flagged as \"unverified until we see a real scanned file\" \u2014 now we've seen it, and it confirms exactly what I predicted: these files have almost no extractable text, so my code correctly detected \"this needs OCR\" and correctly failed because the OCR tools aren't installed yet. Not a design flaw \u2014 a missing install.\n\n## A real bug this run exposed (fixing now)\n\nLook closely at the `needs_review` list \u2014 several `doc_id`s appear **twice or three times** (e.g. `petition_concerning_thorn_wraith` three times). That means two *different* files \u2014 likely the same content in two different formats, e.g. a `.pdf` and a `.docx` version \u2014 are colliding into the same ID. That's a real problem: whichever gets indexed second silently overwrites the first in any lookup. Small fix, but important to catch now, not during grading.\n\nIn `src/ingest/parse_document.py`, find this line:\n```python\ndoc_id = f\"{source_type.value}_{path.stem}_{_slugify(title)}\"\n```\nReplace it with:\n```python\ndoc_id = f\"{source_type.value}_{path.stem}_{path.suffix.lstrip('.')}_{_slugify(title)}\"\n```\n\n## The decision that actually matters now\n```\nThis block is not supported on your current device yet.\n```\n\n", "content": [{"start_timestamp": "2026-08-29T15:48:36.267320Z", "stop_timestamp": "2026-08-29T15:49:26.140743Z", "flags": null, "type": "thinking", "thinking": "This is valuable real data to work through.
