"2026-09-04T11:57:19.029154Z", "flags": null, "type": "tool_use", "id": "toolu_01JbBjwT7kj6ZBt8Wc2tz9w2", "name": "create_file", "input": {"description": "Personal reference guide explaining the whole project simply, for future replication", "path": "/home/claude/ashen-era-build-guide.md", "file_text": "# How I Built a \"Search Like a Human\" AI Agent\n### A personal guide \u2014 for future me, and for anyone I share this with\n\n---\n\n## 0. What is this document?\n\nThis is a plain-English walkthrough of a real project I built: an AI that answers\nquestions by *searching, reading, and deciding* \u2014 the same way a human researcher\nwould, instead of just grabbing the first thing that looks related.\n\nI'm writing this so that:\n- I can rebuild something like this from scratch next time, faster.\n- A friend with zero background can read this and actually understand it.\n- Future me remembers *why* I made each decision, not just *what* I built.\n\nNo prior knowledge assumed. Every technical word gets explained the first time it shows up.\n\n---\n\n## 1. The Big Idea (Explained Like You're Ten)\n\nImagine you have a giant library \u2014 thousands of pages, letters, books, and notes,\nall about a made-up fantasy world. Someone asks you: *\"In what year was this\nmagical gauntlet actually forged?\"*\n\nA **bad** way to answer: open one random book, read one paragraph, blurt out\nwhatever you saw first \u2014 even if it's wrong or only half the story.\n\nA **good** way \u2014 the way a real detective or researcher works:\n1. Search for the thing you're asked about.\n2. Read what you find.\n3. Ask yourself: *\"Do I actually have enough to answer this? Or is something missing,\n   or do two books disagree with each other?\"*\n4. If something's missing or two sources disagree \u2014 go search again, smarter this time.\n5. Once you're actually confident, give your answer \u2014 and if two sources\n   disagreed, explain which one you trusted and why.\n\nThat's the whole project. Everything below is just *how* we taught a computer to do that.\n\n---\n\n## 2. The Big Picture \u2014 All the Pieces, in One Diagram\n\n```\nRAW FILES (docs, pdfs, markdown, images)\n        \u2502\n        \u25bc\n   [1] INGESTION        -- \"read every file, no matter its format\"\n        \u2502\n        \u25bc\n   [2] CHUNKING          -- \"cut long texts into bite-sized pieces\"\n        \u2502\n        \u25bc\n   [3] EMBEDDING+STORAGE -- \"turn each piece into a searchable fingerprint\"\n        \u2502\n        \u25bc\n   [4] AGENT LOOP         -- \"search \u2192 read \u2192 decide: enough, or search again?\"\n        \u2502\n        \u25bc\n   [5] CONFLICT CHECK      -- \"do any sources disagree? who do I trust, and why?\"\n        \u2502\n        \u25bc\n   [6] FINAL ANSWER\n        \u2502\n        \u25bc\n   [7] WEB UI (optional)  -- \"a nice-looking way for a human to ask questions\"\n```\n\nEach numbered stage below is its own section, in the exact order we actually built them.\n\n---\n\n## 3. Tools & Accounts You Need Before Starting\n\n| Tool | What it's for | Why this one |\n|---|---|---|\n| **Python 3.10+** | The programming language everything is written in | Free, huge ecosystem, good for AI work |\n| **An OpenRouter account** (openrouter.ai) | Gives you free access to AI language models AND free \"embedding\" models | No credit card needed, genuinely free tier \u2014 perfect for a student project |\n| **ChromaDB** (a Python package, not a website) | Stores and searches \"fingerprints\" of text on your own computer | Free, runs locally, no server to set up |\n| **Flask** (a Python package) | Turns your Python code into a website | Tiny, simple, no complicated setup |\n| *(Optional)* **tesseract** | Reads text out of images (like a scanned photo of a letter) | We actually decided to SKIP this \u2014 see Section 7 for why |\n\n**A note on money:** everything above costs $0 to start. The only paid step we\nconsidered was adding a small OpenRouter credit top-up ($10) to raise the daily\nfree-usage limit \u2014 optional, not required to build the whole thing.\n\n---\n\n## 4. Project Folder Structure\n\n```\nmy-project/\n\u251c\u2500\u2500 data/\n\u2502   \u251c\u2500\u2500 raw/                  <- your original source files go here\n\u2502   \u2502   \u251c\u2500\u2500 topic-folder-1/   <- e.g. \"wiki\", \"codex\", \"chronicles\"...\n\u2502   \u2502   \u2514\u2500\u2500 topic-folder-2/\n\u2502   \u251c\u2500\u2500 sample_questions.json <- example questions to test against\n\u2502   \u2514\u2500\u2500 processed/            <- the AI's \"memory\" gets stored here (auto-created)\n\u251c\u2500\u2500 src/\n\u2502   \u251c\u2500\u2500 models/       <- defines the \"shape\" of a piece of data\n\u2502   \u251c\u2500\u2500 ingest/        <- reads raw files and turns them into that shape\n\u2502   \u251c\u2500\u2500 chunk/          <- cuts long text into smaller pieces\n\u2502   \u251c\u2500\u2500 embed/           <- turns text into searchable fingerprints\n\u2502   \u251c\u2500\u2500 agent/             <- the actual \"brain\" that searches and answers\n\u2502   \u2514\u2500\u2500 web/                <- optional website on top of it all\n\u251c\u2500\u2500 .env                      <- your secret API key lives here (never shared/committed)\n\u2514\u2500\u2500 .gitignore                 <- tells git to ignore .env and other junk\n```\n\n**Rule of thumb:** every folder under `src/` needs an empty file called\n`__init__.py` inside it \u2014 this is just Python's way of saying \"this folder\ncontains real code, not just random files.\" Easy to forget, causes confusing\n\"module not found\" errors if you do.\n\n---\n\n## 5. Build Order \u2014 Step by Step\n\nThis is the heart of the document. We built things in this exact order because\neach step depends on the one before it. Skipping ahead usually means\nbacktracking later.\n\n### STEP 1 \u2014 Define the \"shape\" of a piece of information\n**File:** `src/models/document.py`\n\n**Kid explanation:** before you can organize a messy room, you need to decide\nwhat a \"box\" looks like \u2014 does it have a label? A size? A category? This file\nis that decision, but for data.\n\n**What it actually does:** defines a `SourceDocument` \u2014 a standard container\nthat every single file, no matter its original format, gets turned into. It\nhas a title, the actual text, and (importantly) a **reliability score** \u2014\na number from 0 to 1 saying how much we should trust this source by default.\n\n**Key idea worth remembering:** if your data comes from sources of different\ntrustworthiness (official records vs. rumors, for example), decide that\nup front, as a number, attached to every piece of text. This one decision\nshapes everything downstream.\n\n```python\nDEFAULT_RELIABILITY = {\n    \"official_record\": 0.9,\n    \"community_notes\": 0.7,\n    \"personal_letters\": 0.3,\n}\n```\n\n---\n\n### STEP 2 \u2014 Teach the code to read every file format\n**File:** `src/ingest/readers.py`\n\n**Kid explanation:** imagine you have books written in English, French, and\nin code \u2014 you need a different translator for each language, but they all\nneed to end up meaning the same thing in your notebook.\n\n**What it does:** one function per file type (`.md`, `.docx`, `.pdf`, `.png`\nimages) that all do the same job \u2014 take a raw file, return plain text out of it.\n\n**Big lesson we learned the hard way:** don't assume \"this folder only has\none file type.\" Real-world data is messy \u2014 a \"chronicles\" folder might have\nboth `.docx` AND `.pdf` files inside it. Keep \"what folder is this in\" and\n\"what format is this file\" as two *completely separate* questions. We\noriginally mixed these up and it caused real bugs.\n\n---\n\n### STEP 3 \u2014 Teach the code to split one file into multiple entries\n**File:** `src/ingest/split.py`\n\n**Kid explanation:** one book might actually contain 20 short stories. You\ndon't want to treat the whole book as \"one story\" \u2014 you want to find where\neach story starts and ends.\n\n**What it does:** looks for heading patterns (like `# Title` in a document)\nand splits the text at those points. Each split piece becomes its own\nseparate `SourceDocument`.\n\n**Big lesson we learned the hard way (this one bit us twice):** don't assume\nevery file uses headings the same way. In our project, most files used one\nheading level per entry \u2014 but ONE file nested things differently (a creature's\nNAME was one heading level, with sub-sections like \"Appearance\" and \"Threat\nLevel\" at a DEEPER heading level underneath it). Our first fix didn't check\ndeep enough levels, so it accidentally split on the sub-section names\ninstead of the creature names \u2014 meaning 10 different creatures' \"Appearance\"\nsections all got treated as ONE mixed-up document.\n\n**The fix, as a reusable rule:** always let the code look at ALL heading\nlevels actually present in a file, and split on the *shallowest* one that\nrepeats \u2014 don't hardcode a guess based on one sample file.\n\n---\n\n### STEP 4 \u2014 Teach the code to find tables inside text\n**File:** `src/ingest/tables.py`\n\n**Kid explanation:** some information isn't a sentence \u2014 it's a chart, like\n\"Name: Sword. Cost: 50 coins.\" This step specifically hunts for that\nchart-shaped information and pulls it out cleanly.\n\n**What it does:** looks for two different table styles (simple `| A | B |`\nstyle, and a fancier boxed style) and turns both into simple `{key: value}`\npairs your code can use directly.\n\n---\n\n### STEP 5 \u2014 Combine \"which folder\" and \"which format\" correctly\n**File:** `src/ingest/parse_document.py`\n\n**Kid explanation:** this is the file that finally says: \"okay, I know HOW to\nread this file (from Step 2), and I know HOW to split it into pieces (from\nStep 3) and find its tables (Step 4) \u2014 now let's actually do all three, in\norder, for one specific file.\"\n\n**What it does:** the \"orchestrator\" \u2014 takes one file path, figures out its\nformat, reads it, splits it, table-extracts it, and returns a clean list of\n`SourceDocument` objects, one per entity/entry found inside.\n\n---\n\n### STEP 6 \u2014 Walk the whole folder and process everything\n**File:** `src/ingest/parse_corpus.py`\n\n**Kid explanation:** now that you know how to process ONE file, this step\njust says \"do that for EVERY file in EVERY folder.\"\n\n**What it does:** loops through every topic folder, every file inside it,\ncalls Step 5 on each one, and collects a full report: how many files worked,\nhow many failed, how many needed manual review.\n\n**Big lesson:** always build a **safety net**. We added logic so that if two\ndifferent files ever accidentally produce the same internal ID, the code\nautomatically renames the second one instead of crashing the entire run.\nSmall insurance policy, saved us real time.\n\n---\n\n### STEP 7 \u2014 Cut long documents into bite-sized pieces\n**File:** `src/chunk/chunker.py`\n\n**Kid explanation:** if a document is a whole book chapter, that's too much\ninformation to hand to the AI in one go \u2014 like trying to memorize an entire\nchapter word-for-word instead of a few key sentences at a time.\n\n**What it does:** short documents (a few paragraphs) stay whole. Long ones\nget cut into ~1000-character pieces, with a little bit of overlap between\npieces so a sentence never gets awkwardly cut in half and lose meaning.\n\n---\n\n### STEP 8 \u2014 Turn text into searchable \"fingerprints\" and store them\n**File:** `src/embed/embed_and_store.py`\n\n**Kid explanation:** imagine turning every sentence into a unique\nfingerprint made of numbers, where SIMILAR sentences have SIMILAR-looking\nfingerprints. That's what \"embedding\" means. Once everything has a\nfingerprint, finding \"similar meaning\" text becomes just... comparing\nfingerprints, which computers are very fast at.\n\n**What it does:**\n1. Sends batches of text chunks to an AI embedding model (through OpenRouter,\n   free).\n2. Gets back a list of numbers (the \"fingerprint\") for each chunk.\n3. Saves everything into ChromaDB \u2014 a simple local database built exactly\n   for searching by fingerprint-similarity.\n\n**Vocabulary check:** \"embedding\" = the fingerprint. \"Vector database\" = a\ndatabase built specifically to store and search these numeric fingerprints\nfast.\n\n---\n\n### STEP 9 \u2014 A quick way to manually test search\n**File:** `src/embed/test_search.py`\n\n**Kid explanation:** before trusting the whole system, just ask it one\nquestion and see what it finds \u2014 like testing a flashlight before walking\ninto a dark room.\n\n**What it does:** takes a typed question, turns it into a fingerprint too,\nand asks ChromaDB \"what's stored that looks similar to THIS fingerprint?\"\n\n---\n\n### STEP 10 \u2014 Give the AI a search tool\n**File:** `src/agent/search_tool.py`\n\n**Kid explanation:** Step 9 built a flashlight. This step hands that\nflashlight to the actual AI so it can use it whenever it wants.\n\n**What it does, and an important upgrade we made:** at first, search only\nworked by \"meaning\" (fingerprint similarity). But we noticed: if someone asks\nabout a specific NAME (like \"Fenspire\"), a human would just search that exact\nword, not rely purely on vague meaning-matching. So we made search do BOTH:\n- fingerprint/meaning search (good for \"what's this about\" questions)\n- exact name search (good for \"does this specific named thing appear\n  anywhere\" questions)\n\n...and merge the results together. This is called **hybrid search**, and\nit's a genuinely reusable trick for almost any search system.\n\n---\n\n### STEP 11 \u2014 Build a specialist that checks for disagreements\n**File:** `src/agent/conflict_agent.py`\n\n**Kid explanation:** imagine you found two books that disagree about\nsomething. Instead of guessing, you'd want a second, careful reader whose\nONLY job is: \"do these two books actually contradict each other, and if so,\nwhich one should I trust, and why?\"\n\n**What it does:** a SEPARATE AI call (different job, different instructions\nfrom the main search-loop) that only runs right before giving a final\nanswer, and only if more than one source was actually used. It checks: do\nthe sources disagree? If a source explicitly claims authority\n(\"this is the official record, other accounts are wrong\"), that explicit\nclaim wins. Otherwise, it falls back to the default trust score from Step 1.\n\n**Why a SEPARATE agent instead of just cramming this into the main loop:**\nspecialization. The main loop's job is broad (\"where do I search next?\").\nThis one's job is narrow and deep (\"do these specific things actually\nconflict?\"). Different jobs deserve different instructions. And running it\n\"only when needed\" (2+ sources) means it doesn't waste time/money on easy\nquestions.\n\n---\n\n### STEP 12 \u2014 Build the main brain: the loop itself\n**File:** `src/agent/agent_loop.py`\n\n**Kid explanation:** this is the actual detective. Search, read, decide,\nrepeat \u2014 exactly like Section 1 described.\n\n**What it does, step by step, each time you ask it a question:**\n1. Look at the question and whatever's been found so far (nothing, at first).\n2. Ask the AI: \"based on this, do you want to SEARCH for more, or ANSWER now?\"\n3. If it says search \u2014 run the search tool (Step 10), add whatever it finds\n   to the pile of evidence, and go back to step 2.\n4. If it says answer \u2014 hand the draft answer + evidence to the conflict\n   specialist (Step 11) to double-check, then return the final answer.\n5. Safety cap: if it searches more than 5 times without deciding, force a\n   final answer rather than looping forever (and burning API calls forever).\n\n**Big lesson:** we originally told the AI to be SUPER short in its reasoning\n(\"one sentence only\") to keep answers clean. That backfired \u2014 it made the\nsystem look like it wasn't really \"thinking,\" when actually it was, we just\ncouldn't see it. The fix: keep the reasoning short but VISIBLE (2-3\nsentences), while keeping the actual final ANSWER short and clean\nseparately. Don't confuse \"the answer should be short\" with \"the thinking\nshould be invisible\" \u2014 they're different things, and hiding the thinking\nundersells the whole point of a system like this.\n\n---\n\n### STEP 13 \u2014 Make the terminal output pleasant to look at\n**File:** `src/agent/cli_theme.py`\n\n**Kid explanation:** purely cosmetic \u2014 colors, spacing, a little animated\nloading icon while it thinks, so watching it work isn't a wall of grey text.\n\n**What it does:** small helper functions for colored/formatted printing, plus\na simple animation (using a background thread) that plays while a slow\nnetwork request is happening, so the terminal doesn't look frozen.\n\n---\n\n### STEP 14 \u2014 Test on many questions at once, automatically\n**File:** `src/agent/batch_test.py`\n\n**Kid explanation:** instead of asking one question at a time by hand, run\nyour whole exam sheet through the system in one go and save every answer to\nreview later.\n\n**What it does:** loads a list of test questions from a file, runs each one\nthrough Step 12's loop, and saves everything (questions, answers, confidence,\nwhether a conflict was caught, how many search steps it took) into one\nresults file you can look through.\n\n**Why this step matters so much:** it's tempting to build the whole system\nand only test it on ONE hand-picked question that you know will work. Don't.\nTesting at scale is what actually tells you whether your system is solid or\njust got lucky once. We learned this lesson the hard way \u2014 we almost skipped\nstraight to building a nice-looking website before ever running the real\ntest question set.\n\n---\n\n### STEP 15 \u2014 (Optional) Build a simple website on top\n**Files:** `src/web/app.py`, `src/web/templates/index.html`, `src/web/static/style.css`\n\n**Kid explanation:** everything above works fine typed into a terminal. This\nstep just wraps it in a nice-looking webpage so anyone (not just someone\ncomfortable typing commands) can use it.\n\n**What each file does:**\n- `app.py` \u2014 a tiny web server (using Flask). It has one job: receive a\n  question from the webpage, run it through Step 12's loop, send back the\n  answer as data the webpage can display.\n- `index.html` \u2014 the actual page layout: a text box to type your question, a\n  button, and an area where the answer appears.\n- `style.css` \u2014 all the visual styling (colors, fonts, spacing, any theme/\n  animation you want) \u2014 completely separate from the logic, on purpose, so\n  you can restyle the whole look without touching how anything actually works.\n\n**Important ordering lesson:** build this LAST, only once the actual\n\"brain\" underneath is tested and trustworthy. A pretty interface on top of a\nbroken or unverified system just hides the problems \u2014 it doesn't fix them.\n\n---\n\n## 6. How to Run Everything, Start to Finish\n\n```bash\n# one-time setup\npip install pdfplumber python-docx pytesseract pillow openai chromadb python-dotenv flask colorama\n\n# create a file called .env in your project folder containing:\n#   OPENROUTER_API_KEY=your-key-here\n\n# 1. put your raw files into data/raw/<topic-folders>/\n\n# 2. process every file into clean structured data\npython -m src.ingest.parse_corpus\n\n# 3. cut into pieces + turn into searchable fingerprints + store them\npython -m src.embed.embed_and_store\n\n# 4. ask it a single question, see it think out loud\npython -m src.agent.agent_loop \"your question here\"\n\n# 5. run it against a whole batch of test questions\npython -m src.agent.batch_test\n\n# 6. (optional) launch the website version\npython -m src.web.app\n# then open http://127.0.0.1:5000 in your browser\n```\n\n---\n\n## 7. Lessons Worth Remembering For Next Time\n\n- **Format and category are two different questions.** Never assume \"this\n  folder only has one file type.\" Check file extensions independently of\n  which folder something's in.\n- **Don't trust one sample to represent the whole dataset's structure.**\n  Real data is inconsistent \u2014 the same \"type\" of document can be formatted\n  completely differently file to file. Build things to detect structure\n  dynamically instead of hardcoding assumptions from the first example you saw.\n- **Clear your Python cache after editing files** (especially on Windows) \u2014\n  `__pycache__` folders can silently keep running your OLD code even after\n  you save changes, and the error messages you get make it look like the\n  fix didn't work when it actually did.\n- **Free API tiers usually have a daily limit**, not just a \"free forever, no\n  limits\" deal. Know the number before you plan a big batch-test run around it.\n- **Attach a trust/reliability score to your data sources from day one** if\n  they vary in trustworthiness. It's much easier to build this in from the\n  start than bolt it on later.\n- **Let the AI say \"I don't know.\"** A forced guess that's wrong is worse\n  than an honest \"I couldn't find enough evidence.\"\n- **A second, narrow-purpose AI agent, invoked only when actually needed,**\n  is a genuinely useful pattern \u2014 better than either (a) one AI doing\n  everything, or (b) multiple agents running on every single request whether\n  they're needed or not.\n- **Hybrid search (meaning + exact match) beats pure meaning-based search**\n  whenever your data has specific names, numbers, or exact terms that matter.\n- **Build the pretty interface LAST.** Verify the actual logic works first.\n\n---\n\n## 8. Reusing This For a Completely Different Project\n\nThe architecture here isn't specific to fantasy archives \u2014 it works for\n*any* situation where you have a pile of documents from sources of varying\ntrust, and you want an AI to research through them properly instead of\nguessing from one lucky search.\n\n**To reuse this for something new, keep:**\n- The overall pipeline shape (ingest \u2192 chunk \u2192 embed \u2192 search \u2192 decide \u2192 answer)\n- The reliability-tiering idea, if your new data also varies in trustworthiness\n- The hybrid search approach\n- The \"separate specialist for conflict-checking\" pattern\n- The \"let it say I don't know\" principle\n\n**What you'll need to change:**\n- The actual file readers, if your new data uses different formats\n- The reliability tier values (and whether you need them at all)\n- The system prompts (the instructions given to the AI) \u2014 these should\n  describe YOUR new domain, not this fantasy world\n- The UI theme/styling, if you want a different look\n\n---\n\n## 9. Quick Glossary\n\n- **Embedding** \u2014 turning text into a list of numbers (\"fingerprint\") that\n  captures its meaning, so similar text has similar numbers.\n- **Vector database** \u2014 a database built specifically to store and quickly\n  search these number-fingerprints.\n- **Chunk** \u2014 a small, bite-sized piece of a larger document.\n- **RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation)** \u2014 a fancy term for \"let the AI\n  search real documents before answering, instead of only using what it\n  already knows.\"\n- **Agent** \u2014 an AI that can take multiple steps and make decisions on its\n  own (like \"search again\" or \"answer now\"), instead of just answering once.\n- **Hallucination** \u2014 when an AI confidently states something false because\n  it wasn't grounded in real source material.\n- **API key** \u2014 a secret password that lets your code use an AI service.\n  Never share it or upload it to a public place (like GitHub) \u2014 that's what\n  the `.env` file + `.gitignore` combo is for.\n- **Token** \u2014 roughly, a chunk of a word. AI services often charge or limit\n  usage by token count.\n- **Hybrid search** \u2014 combining \"search by meaning\" with \"search by exact\n  match\" and merging the results.\n"}, "message": "Personal reference guide explaining the whole project simply, for future replication", "integration_name": "File Creation", "integration_icon_url": null, "tool_identifier": null, "icon_name": "file", "context": null, "display_content": {"type": "code_block", "language": "markdown", "code": "# How I Built a \"Search Like a Human\" AI Agent\n### A personal guide \u2014 for future me, and for anyone I share this with\n\n---\n\n## 0. What is this document?\n\nThis is a plain-English walkthrough of a real project I built: an AI that answers\nquestions by *searching, reading, and deciding* \u2014 the same way a human researcher\nwould, instead of just grabbing the first thing that looks related.\n\nI'm writing this so that:\n- I can rebuild something like this from scratch next time, faster.\n- A friend with zero background can read this and actually understand it.\n- Future me remembers *why* I made each decision, not just *what* I built.\n\nNo prior knowledge assumed. Every technical word gets explained the first time it shows up.\n\n---\n\n## 1. The Big Idea (Explained Like You're Ten)\n\nImagine you have a giant library \u2014 thousands of pages, letters, books, and notes,\nall about a made-up fantasy world. Someone asks you: *\"In what year was this\nmagical gauntlet actually forged?\"*\n\nA **bad** way to answer: open one random book, read one paragraph, blurt out\nwhatever you saw first \u2014 even if it's wrong or only half the story.\n\nA **good** way \u2014 the way a real detective or researcher works:\n1. Search for the thing you're asked about.\n2. Read what you find.\n3. Ask yourself: *\"Do I actually have enough to answer this? Or is something missing,\n   or do two books disagree with each other?\"*\n4. If something's missing or two sources disagree \u2014 go search again, smarter this time.\n5. Once you're actually confident, give your answer \u2014 and if two sources\n   disagreed, explain which one you trusted and why.\n\nThat's the whole project. Everything below is just *how* we taught a computer to do that.\n\n---\n\n## 2. The Big Picture \u2014 All the Pieces, in One Diagram\n\n```\nRAW FILES (docs, pdfs, markdown, images)\n        \u2502\n        \u25bc\n   [1] INGESTION        -- \"read every file, no matter its format\"\n        \u2502\n        \u25bc\n   [2] CHUNKING          -- \"cut long texts into bite-sized pieces\"\n        \u2502\n        \u25bc\n   [3] EMBEDDING+STORAGE -- \"turn each piece into a searchable fingerprint\"\n        \u2502\n        \u25bc\n   [4] AGENT LOOP         -- \"search \u2192 read \u2192 decide: enough, or search again?\"\n        \u2502\n        \u25bc\n   [5] CONFLICT CHECK      -- \"do any sources disagree? who do I trust, and why?\"\n        \u2502\n        \u25bc\n   [6] FINAL ANSWER\n        \u2502\n        \u25bc\n   [7] WEB UI (optional)  -- \"a nice-looking way for a human to ask questions\"\n```\n\nEach numbered stage below is its own section, in the exact order we actually built them.\n\n---\n\n## 3. Tools & Accounts You Need Before Starting\n\n| Tool | What it's for | Why this one |\n|---|---|---|\n| **Python 3.10+** | The programming language everything is written in | Free, huge ecosystem, good for AI work |\n| **An OpenRouter account** (openrouter.ai) | Gives you free access to AI language models AND free \"embedding\" models | No credit card needed, genuinely free tier \u2014 perfect for a student project |\n| **ChromaDB** (a Python package, not a website) | Stores and searches \"fingerprints\" of text on your own computer | Free, runs locally, no server to set up |\n| **Flask** (a Python package) | Turns your Python code into a website | Tiny, simple, no complicated setup |\n| *(Optional)* **tesseract** | Reads text out of images (like a scanned photo of a letter) | We actually decided to SKIP this \u2014 see Section 7 for why |\n\n**A note on money:** everything above costs $0 to start. The only paid step we\nconsidered was adding a small OpenRouter credit top-up ($10) to raise the daily\nfree-usage limit \u2014 optional, not required to build the whole thing.\n\n---\n\n## 4. Project Folder Structure\n\n```\nmy-project/\n\u251c\u2500\u2500 data/\n\u2502   \u251c\u2500\u2500 raw/                  <- your original source files go here\n\u2502   \u2502   \u251c\u2500\u2500 topic-folder-1/   <- e.g. \"wiki\", \"codex\", \"chronicles\"...\n\u2502   \u2502   \u2514\u2500\u2500 topic-folder-2/\n\u2502   \u251c\u2500\u2500 sample_questions.json <- example questions to test against\n\u2502   \u2514\u2500\u2500 processed/            <- the AI's \"memory\" gets stored here (auto-created)\n\u251c\u2500\u2500 src/\n\u2502   \u251c\u2500\u2500 models/       <- defines the \"shape\" of a piece of data\n\u2502   \u251c\u2500\u2500 ingest/        <- reads raw files and turns them into that shape\n\u2502   \u251c\u2500\u2500 chunk/          <- cuts long text into smaller pieces\n\u2502   \u251c\u2500\u2500 embed/           <- turns text into searchable fingerprints\n\u2502   \u251c\u2500\u2500 agent/             <- the actual \"brain\" that searches and answers\n\u2502   \u2514\u2500\u2500 web/                <- optional website on top of it all\n\u251c\u2500\u2500 .env                      <- your secret API key lives here (never shared/committed)\n\u2514\u2500\u2500 .gitignore                 <- tells git to ignore .env and other junk\n```\n\n**Rule of thumb:** every folder under `src/` needs an empty file called\n`__init__.py` inside it \u2014 this is just Python's way of saying \"this folder\ncontains real code, not just random files.\" Easy to forget, causes confusing\n\"module not found\" errors if you do.\n\n---\n\n## 5. Build Order \u2014 Step by Step\n\nThis is the heart of the document. We built things in this exact order because\neach step depends on the one before it. Skipping ahead usually means\nbacktracking later.\n\n### STEP 1 \u2014 Define the \"shape\" of a piece of information\n**File:** `src/models/document.py`\n\n**Kid explanation:** before you can organize a messy room, you need to decide\nwhat a \"box\" looks like \u2014 does it have a label? A size? A category? This file\nis that decision, but for data.\n\n**What it actually does:** defines a `SourceDocument` \u2014 a standard container\nthat every single file, no matter its original format, gets turned into. It\nhas a title, the actual text, and (importantly) a **reliability score** \u2014\na number from 0 to 1 saying how much we should trust this source by default.\n\n**Key idea worth remembering:** if your data comes from sources of different\ntrustworthiness (official records vs. rumors, for example), decide that\nup front, as a number, attached to every piece of text. This one decision\nshapes everything downstream.\n\n```python\nDEFAULT_RELIABILITY = {\n    \"official_record\": 0.9,\n    \"community_notes\": 0.7,\n    \"personal_letters\": 0.3,\n}\n```\n\n---\n\n### STEP 2 \u2014 Teach the code to read every file format\n**File:** `src/ingest/readers.py`\n\n**Kid explanation:** imagine you have books written in English, French, and\nin code \u2014 you need a different translator for each language, but they all\nneed to end up meaning the same thing in your notebook.\n\n**What it does:** one function per file type (`.md`, `.docx`, `.pdf`, `.png`\nimages) that all do the same job \u2014 take a raw file, return plain text out of it.\n\n**Big lesson we learned the hard way:** don't assume \"this folder only has\none file type.\" Real-world data is messy \u2014 a \"chronicles\" folder might have\nboth `.docx` AND `.pdf` files inside it. Keep \"what folder is this in\" and\n\"what format is this file\" as two *completely separate* questions. We\noriginally mixed these up and it caused real bugs.\n\n---\n\n### STEP 3 \u2014 Teach the code to split one file into multiple entries\n**File:** `src/ingest/split.py`\n\n**Kid explanation:** one book might actually contain 20 short stories. You\ndon't want to treat the whole book as \"one story\" \u2014 you want to find where\neach story starts and ends.\n\n**What it does:** looks for heading patterns (like `# Title` in a document)\nand splits the text at those points. Each split piece becomes its own\nseparate `SourceDocument`.\n\n**Big lesson we learned the hard way (this one bit us twice):** don't assume\nevery file uses headings the same way. In our project, most files used one\nheading level per entry \u2014 but ONE file nested things differently (a creature's\nNAME was one heading level, with sub-sections like \"Appearance\" and \"Threat\nLevel\" at a DEEPER heading level underneath it). Our first fix didn't check\ndeep enough levels, so it accidentally split on the sub-section names\ninstead of the creature names \u2014 meaning 10 different creatures' \"Appearance\"\nsections all got treated as ONE mixed-up document.\n\n**The fix, as a reusable rule:** always let the code look at ALL heading\nlevels actually present in a file, and split on the *shallowest* one that\nrepeats \u2014 don't hardcode a guess based on one sample file.\n\n---\n\n### STEP 4 \u2014 Teach the code to find tables inside text\n**File:** `src/ingest/tables.py`\n\n**Kid explanation:** some information isn't a sentence \u2014 it's a chart, like\n\"Name: Sword. Cost: 50 coins.\" This step specifically hunts for that\nchart-shaped information and pulls it out cleanly.\n\n**What it does:** looks for two different table styles (simple `| A | B |`\nstyle, and a fancier boxed style) and turns both into simple `{key: value}`\npairs your code can use directly.\n\n---\n\n### STEP 5 \u2014 Combine \"which folder\" and \"which format\" correctly\n**File:** `src/ingest/parse_document.py`\n\n**Kid explanation:** this is the file that finally says: \"okay, I know HOW to\nread this file (from Step 2), and I know HOW to split it into pieces (from\nStep 3) and find its tables (Step 4) \u2014 now let's actually do all three, in\norder, for one specific file.\"\n\n**What it does:** the \"orchestrator\" \u2014 takes one file path, figures out its\nformat, reads it, splits it, table-extracts it, and returns a clean list of\n`SourceDocument` objects, one per entity/entry found inside.\n\n---\n\n### STEP 6 \u2014 Walk the whole folder and process everything\n**File:** `src/ingest/parse_corpus.py`\n\n**Kid explanation:** now that you know how to process ONE file, this step\njust says \"do that for EVERY file in EVERY folder.\"\n\n**What it does:** loops through every topic folder, every file inside it,\ncalls Step 5 on each one, and collects a full report: how many files worked,\nhow many failed, how many needed manual review.\n\n**Big lesson:** always build a **safety net**. We added logic so that if two\ndifferent files ever accidentally produce the same internal ID, the code\nautomatically renames the second one instead of crashing the entire run.\nSmall insurance policy, saved us real time.\n\n---\n\n### STEP 7 \u2014 Cut long documents into bite-sized pieces\n**File:** `src/chunk/chunker.py`\n\n**Kid explanation:** if a document is a whole book chapter, that's too much\ninformation to hand to the AI in one go \u2014 like trying to memorize an entire\nchapter word-for-word instead of a few key sentences at a time.\n\n**What it does:** short documents (a few paragraphs) stay whole. Long ones\nget cut into ~1000-character pieces, with a little bit of overlap between\npieces so a sentence never gets awkwardly cut in half and lose meaning.\n\n---\n\n### STEP 8 \u2014 Turn text into searchable \"fingerprints\" and store them\n**File:** `src/embed/embed_and_store.py`\n\n**Kid explanation:** imagine turning every sentence into a unique\nfingerprint made of numbers, where SIMILAR sentences have SIMILAR-looking\nfingerprints. That's what \"embedding\" means. Once everything has a\nfingerprint, finding \"similar meaning\" text becomes just... comparing\nfingerprints, which computers are very fast at.\n\n**What it does:**\n1. Sends batches of text chunks to an AI embedding model (through OpenRouter,\n   free).\n2. Gets back a list of numbers (the \"fingerprint\") for each chunk.\n3. Saves everything into ChromaDB \u2014 a simple local database built exactly\n   for searching by fingerprint-similarity.\n\n**Vocabulary check:** \"embedding\" = the fingerprint. \"Vector database\" = a\ndatabase built specifically to store and search these numeric fingerprints\nfast.\n\n---\n\n### STEP 9 \u2014 A quick way to manually test search\n**File:** `src/embed/test_search.py`\n\n**Kid explanation:** before trusting the whole system, just ask it one\nquestion and see what it finds \u2014 like testing a flashlight before walking\ninto a dark room.\n\n**What it does:** takes a typed question, turns it into a fingerprint too,\nand asks ChromaDB \"what's stored that looks similar to THIS fingerprint?\"\n\n---\n\n### STEP 10 \u2014 Give the AI a search tool\n**File:** `src/agent/search_tool.py`\n\n**Kid explanation:** Step 9 built a flashlight. This step hands that\nflashlight to the actual AI so it can use it whenever it wants.\n\n**What it does, and an important upgrade we made:** at first, search only\nworked by \"meaning\" (fingerprint similarity). But we noticed: if someone asks\nabout a specific NAME (like \"Fenspire\"), a human would just search that exact\nword, not rely purely on vague meaning-matching. So we made search do BOTH:\n- fingerprint/meaning search (good for \"what's this about\" questions)\n- exact name search (good for \"does this specific named thing appear\n  anywhere\" questions)\n\n...and merge the results together. This is called **hybrid search**, and\nit's a genuinely reusable trick for almost any search system.\n\n---\n\n### STEP 11 \u2014 Build a specialist that checks for disagreements\n**File:** `src/agent/conflict_agent.py`\n\n**Kid explanation:** imagine you found two books that disagree about\nsomething. Instead of guessing, you'd want a second, careful reader whose\nONLY job is: \"do these two books actually contradict each other, and if so,\nwhich one should I trust, and why?\"\n\n**What it does:** a SEPARATE AI call (different job, different instructions\nfrom the main search-loop) that only runs right before giving a final\nanswer, and only if more than one source was actually used. It checks: do\nthe sources disagree? If a source explicitly claims authority\n(\"this is the official record, other accounts are wrong\"), that explicit\nclaim wins. Otherwise, it falls back to the default trust score from Step 1.\n\n**Why a SEPARATE agent instead of just cramming this into the main loop:**\nspecialization. The main loop's job is broad (\"where do I search next?\").\nThis one's job is narrow and deep (\"do these specific things actually\nconflict?\"). Different jobs deserve different instructions. And running it\n\"only when needed\" (2+ sources) means it doesn't waste time/money on easy\nquestions.\n\n---\n\n### STEP 12 \u2014 Build the main brain: the loop itself\n**File:** `src/agent/agent_loop.py`\n\n**Kid explanation:** this is the actual detective. Search, read, decide,\nrepeat \u2014 exactly like Section 1 described.\n\n**What it does, step by step, each time you ask it a question:**\n1. Look at the question and whatever's been found so far (nothing, at first).\n2. Ask the AI: \"based on this, do you want to SEARCH for more, or ANSWER now?\"\n3. If it says search \u2014 run the search tool (Step 10), add whatever it finds\n   to the pile of evidence, and go back to step 2.\n4. If it says answer \u2014 hand the draft answer + evidence to the conflict\n   specialist (Step 11) to double-check, then return the final answer.\n5. Safety cap: if it searches more than 5 times without deciding, force a\n   final answer rather than looping forever (and burning API calls forever).\n\n**Big lesson:** we originally told the AI to be SUPER short in its reasoning\n(\"one sentence only\") to keep answers clean. That backfired \u2014 it made the\nsystem look like it wasn't really \"thinking,\" when actually it was, we just\ncouldn't see it. The fix: keep the reasoning short but VISIBLE (2-3\nsentences), while keeping the actual final ANSWER short and clean\nseparately. Don't confuse \"the answer should be short\" with \"the thinking\nshould be invisible\" \u2014 they're different things, and hiding the thinking\nundersells the whole point of a system like this.\n\n---\n\n### STEP 13 \u2014 Make the terminal output pleasant to look at\n**File:** `src/agent/cli_theme.py`\n\n**Kid explanation:** purely cosmetic \u2014 colors, spacing, a little animated\nloading icon while it thinks, so watching it work isn't a wall of grey text.\n\n**What it does:** small helper functions for colored/formatted printing, plus\na simple animation (using a background thread) that plays while a slow\nnetwork request is happening, so the terminal doesn't look frozen.\n\n---\n\n### STEP 14 \u2014 Test on many questions at once, automatically\n**File:** `src/agent/batch_test.py`\n\n**Kid explanation:** instead of asking one question at a time by hand, run\nyour whole exam sheet through the system in one go and save every answer to\nreview later.\n\n**What it does:** loads a list of test questions from a file, runs each one\nthrough Step 12's loop, and saves everything (questions, answers, confidence,\nwhether a conflict was caught, how many search steps it took) into one\nresults file you can look through.\n\n**Why this step matters so much:** it's tempting to build the whole system\nand only test it on ONE hand-picked question that you know will work. Don't.\nTesting at scale is what actually tells you whether your system is solid or\njust got lucky once. We learned this lesson the hard way \u2014 we almost skipped\nstraight to building a nice-looking website before ever running the real\ntest question set.\n\n---\n\n### STEP 15 \u2014 (Optional) Build a simple website on top\n**Files:** `src/web/app.py`, `src/web/templates/index.html`, `src/web/static/style.css`\n\n**Kid explanation:** everything above works fine typed into a terminal. This\nstep just wraps it in a nice-looking webpage so anyone (not just someone\ncomfortable typing commands) can use it.\n\n**What each file does:**\n- `app.py` \u2014 a tiny web server (using Flask). It has one job: receive a\n  question from the webpage, run it through Step 12's loop, send back the\n  answer as data the webpage can display.\n- `index.html` \u2014 the actual page layout: a text box to type your question, a\n  button, and an area where the answer appears.\n- `style.css` \u2014 all the visual styling (colors, fonts, spacing, any theme/\n  animation you want) \u2014 completely separate from the logic, on purpose, so\n  you can restyle the whole look without touching how anything actually works.\n\n**Important ordering lesson:** build this LAST, only once the actual\n\"brain\" underneath is tested and trustworthy. A pretty interface on top of a\nbroken or unverified system just hides the problems \u2014 it doesn't fix them.\n\n---\n\n## 6. How to Run Everything, Start to Finish\n\n```bash\n# one-time setup\npip install pdfplumber python-docx pytesseract pillow openai chromadb python-dotenv flask colorama\n\n# create a file called .env in your project folder containing:\n#   OPENROUTER_API_KEY=your-key-here\n\n# 1. put your raw files into data/raw/<topic-folders>/\n\n# 2. process every file into clean structured data\npython -m src.ingest.parse_corpus\n\n# 3. cut into pieces + turn into searchable fingerprints + store them\npython -m src.embed.embed_and_store\n\n# 4. ask it a single question, see it think out loud\npython -m src.agent.agent_loop \"your question here\"\n\n# 5. run it against a whole batch of test questions\npython -m src.agent.batch_test\n\n# 6. (optional) launch the website version\npython -m src.web.app\n# then open http://127.0.0.1:5000 in your browser\n```\n\n---\n\n## 7. Lessons Worth Remembering For Next Time\n\n- **Format and category are two different questions.** Never assume \"this\n  folder only has one file type.\" Check file extensions independently of\n  which folder something's in.\n- **Don't trust one sample to represent the whole dataset's structure.**\n  Real data is inconsistent \u2014 the same \"type\" of document can be formatted\n  completely differently file to file. Build things to detect structure\n  dynamically instead of hardcoding assumptions from the first example you saw.\n- **Clear your Python cache after editing files** (especially on Windows) \u2014\n  `__pycache__` folders can silently keep running your OLD code even after\n  you save changes, and the error messages you get make it look like the\n  fix didn't work when it actually did.\n- **Free API tiers usually have a daily limit**, not just a \"free forever, no\n  limits\" deal. Know the number before you plan a big batch-test run around it.\n- **Attach a trust/reliability score to your data sources from day one** if\n  they vary in trustworthiness. It's much easier to build this in from the\n  start than bolt it on later.\n- **Let the AI say \"I don't know.\"** A forced guess that's wrong is worse\n  than an honest \"I couldn't find enough evidence.\"\n- **A second, narrow-purpose AI agent, invoked only when actually needed,**\n  is a genuinely useful pattern \u2014 better than either (a) one AI doing\n  everything, or (b) multiple agents running on every single request whether\n  they're needed or not.\n- **Hybrid search (meaning + exact match) beats pure meaning-based search**\n  whenever your data has specific names, numbers, or exact terms that matter.\n- **Build the pretty interface LAST.** Verify the actual logic works first.\n\n---\n\n## 8. Reusing This For a Completely Different Project\n\nThe architecture here isn't specific to fantasy archives \u2014 it works for\n*any* situation where you have a pile of documents from sources of varying\ntrust, and you want an AI to research through them properly instead of\nguessing from one lucky search.\n\n**To reuse this for something new, keep:**\n- The overall pipeline shape (ingest \u2192 chunk \u2192 embed \u2192 search \u2192 decide \u2192 answer)\n- The reliability-tiering idea, if your new data also varies in trustworthiness\n- The hybrid search approach\n- The \"separate specialist for conflict-checking\" pattern\n- The \"let it say I don't know\" principle\n\n**What you'll need to change:**\n- The actual file readers, if your new data uses different formats\n- The reliability tier values (and whether you need them at all)\n- The system prompts (the instructions given to the AI) \u2014 these should\n  describe YOUR new domain, not this fantasy world\n- The UI theme/styling, if you want a different look\n\n---\n\n## 9. Quick Glossary\n\n- **Embedding** \u2014 turning text into a list of numbers (\"fingerprint\") that\n  captures its meaning, so similar text has similar numbers.\n- **Vector database** \u2014 a database built specifically to store and quickly\n  search these number-fingerprints.\n- **Chunk** \u2014 a small, bite-sized piece of a larger document.\n- **RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation)** \u2014 a fancy term for \"let the AI\n  search real documents before answering, instead of only using what it\n  already knows.\"\n- **Agent** \u2014 an AI that can take multiple steps and make decisions on its\n  own (like \"search again\" or \"answer now\"), instead of just answering once.\n- **Hallucination** \u2014 when an AI confidently states something false because\n  it wasn't grounded in real source material.\n- **API key** \u2014 a secret password that lets your code use an AI service.\n  Never share it or upload it to a public place (like GitHub) \u2014 that's what\n  the `.env` file + `.gitignore` combo is for.\n- **Token** \u2014 roughly, a chunk of a word. AI services often charge or limit\n  usage by token count.\n- **Hybrid search** \u2014 combining \"search by meaning\" with \"search by exact\n  match\" and merging the results.\n", "filename": Where teams will actually separate is in the details most won't bother with. Two things stand out to me as genuinely distinctive (not cosmetic) and buildable in the time you have:\n\n**A. Actually use the entity links you're already extracting.** Remember the wiki files have `[[Fenspire]]`-style links? We extract these during ingestion but currently throw them away after that. A human researcher doesn't just re-search blindly each iteration \u2014 they follow the citation/link they just found. We could make the agent's next search genuinely informed by explicit entity relationships discovered in the previous step (e.g., found \"Ederon is a member of [[Iron-Ring Cartel]]\" \u2192 next search is seeded with that exact link, not just re-guessed by the LLM). This is a real technical upgrade to \"search like a human,\" not just a talking point.\n\n**B. Ground the \"sources\" claim, don't just trust the LLM's word for it.** Right now, when the agent says `\"sources\": [\"Codex Vaeloria I - Ashreach\"]`, that's just text the model typed \u2014 nothing verifies it actually matches a chunk it really retrieved. A cheap, valuable addition: cross-check claimed sources against the actual evidence gathered, and flag it if the model cites something it never really looked at. We built an agent that performs this\nloop explicitly rather than doing a single retrieve-then-answer pass.\n\n## Pipeline\n\n```\nRaw corpus (mixed formats, mixed topics)\n        \u2502\n        \u25bc\nIngestion (src/ingest/) \u2014 format-agnostic readers (.md/.docx/.pdf), decoupled\n        \u2502                  from topic folder. Single sub-track (1C), not combined with 1B\nInitially considered combining 1C and 1B as a multi-agent system. Dropped this \u2014\nthe challenge doc explicitly states a strong single-track solution beats a shallow\nmulti-track one. Discovered during testing that a well-built 1C loop generalizes\nto 1B-style multi-hop questions as an emergent property (validated: 7/7 real\n1B-tagged sample questions answered correctly via multi-step chaining), without\nneeding separate architecture.\n\n## 2. Stack: OpenRouter + ChromaDB, not Voyage AI or Grok\nVoyage AI requires a card for identity verification (even though free-tier usage\nitself is free) \u2014 ruled out under a strict no-card constraint. Grok's API has no\ngenuine free tier (pay-per-token, plus an opt-in data-sharing free-credit program\nwe didn't want to depend on). OpenRouter's free embedding + free chat models\nrequire no card at all and were sufficient for this project's scale.\n\n## 3. Reliability tiering as a first-class design element\nSource type determines a default trust prior (codex 0.9 > wiki 0.7 > chronicle\n0.5 > ephemera 0.3), attached to every chunk at ingestion time. This was driven\ndirectly by corpus evidence: the codex explicitly states things like \"this is the\nauthoritative record, popular accounts wrongly claim otherwise\" \u2014 a strong signal\nthat source trust needed to be reasoned over, not assumed uniform.\n\n## 4. Format decoupled from topic folder\nEarly implementation assumed each topic folder (codex/chronicles/ephemera) used\none consistent file format. This was wrong \u2014 the real corpus mixes .docx and .pdf\nwithin the same topic. Fixed by treating \"which folder\" (topic/reliability) and\n\"which file extension\" (how to read it) as fully independent decisions.\n\n## 5. OCR disabled by default\nStandalone images and scanned PDFs require OCR (tesseract). This was tested and\ntechnically works, but is slow on typical development hardware and low-value for\nthis specific track \u2014 1C's fact-lookup questions are answerable from text sources\n(the same facts on image figure-plates typically also appear in codex register\ntables). Documented as a deliberate trade-off, not an oversight \u2014 see limitations.md.\n\n## 6. Hybrid search (semantic + exact match)\nPure vector similarity search can miss exact named-entity queries when phrasing\ndiffers from the source text. Added exact substring matching for capitalized\nproper-noun candidates extracted from each query, merged with semantic results.\n\n## 7. Honest uncertainty over forced answers\nThe agent can respond \"insufficient evidence\" instead of guessing. A wrong\nconfident answer is worse than an honest gap, especially for a system meant to\ndemonstrate calibrated reasoning rather than just producing text.\n\n## 8. A separate conflict-resolution agent, invoked adaptively\nRather than folding conflict-checking into every single decision (expensive) or\nnever checking at all (risks confidently wrong answers on contested facts), a\nsecond agent with a narrowly-scoped prompt runs only when 2+ distinct sources\nwere used to answer. This was implemented (tesseract + pymupdf) and functions,\nbut is disabled by default (`SKIP_OCR = True` in `src/ingest/parse_corpus.py`)\nbecause it is slow on typical development hardware and most of the affected\ncontent (character portraits, faction heraldry, creature art) is more relevant\nto sub-track 1A's image-embedding requirement than to 1C's fact-lookup nature.\nWhere figure plates encode numeric facts (attunement costs, garrison strength),\nthose same facts typically also exist in codex register tables already captured\nas text. Risk of missing information is assessed as low but non-zero for our track.\n\n## No dedicated 1B architecture\nThe system was not purpose-built for multi-document fact-linking. Its strong\nperformance on 1B-style sample questions (7/7 answered via correct multi-hop\nchaining) is an emergent property of a well-built 1C search loop, not a\ndeliberately engineered second capability. No entity graph or explicit\nmulti-document synthesis logic exists.\n\n## No ground-truth answer verification\nBatch test results were verified for *mechanism* (did it search iteratively,\nchain correctly, catch conflicts) but not independently fact-checked against\nthe source documents question-by-question. Time constraints (mid-semester\nexams during the build window) limited manual verification depth.\n\n## Free-tier API rate limits\nOpenRouter's free tier caps at 50 requests/day without a credit top-up. Each\nagent iteration costs 2 API calls (embedding + decision), plus a conditional\nconflict-check call \u2014 meaning a single batch of ~7 multi-hop questions can\nconsume the entire daily allowance. This constrained how much large-scale\ntesting could be done per day during development.\n\n## Approaches tried and abandoned\n- **Combining 1B and 1C as a multi-agent system** \u2014 dropped in favor of a single\n  well-built 1C loop, per explicit competition guidance rewarding depth over\n  breadth.\n- **Voyage AI and Grok for embeddings/LLM** \u2014 both required either a card\n  (Voyage) or had no genuine free tier (Grok); replaced with OpenRouter.\n- **Pandoc for .docx parsing** \u2014 required an external system dependency with\n  Windows installation friction; replaced with native python-docx parsing.\n- **A fixed heading-level assumption for document splitting** \u2014 an early version\n  assumed one heading level marked entity boundaries across all files. Real\n  corpus files use inconsistent heading depths (entity name at one level,\n  sub-sections nested one level deeper in some files but not others). Fixed by\n  detecting the shallowest heading level actually present per file, rather than\n  hardcoding an assumption from a single sample file.\n", "path": "/home/claude/ashen-agent/docs/limitations.md"}, "message": "Honest limitations and what was tried and rejected", "integration_name": "File Creation", "integration_icon_url": null, "tool_identifier": null, "icon_name": "file", "context": null, "display_content": {"type": "code_block", "language": "markdown", "code": "# Limitations \u2014 Ashen Era Archive Assistant\n\n## OCR is disabled by default\n~87 of the corpus's 415 files (standalone images and `.scan.pdf` files) require\nOCR to extract text. This was implemented (tesseract + pymupdf) and functions,\nbut is disabled by default (`SKIP_OCR = True` in `src/ingest/parse_corpus.py`)\nbecause it is slow on typical development hardware and most of the affected\ncontent (character portraits, faction heraldry, creature art) is more relevant\nto sub-track 1A's image-embedding requirement than to 1C's fact-lookup nature.\nWhere figure plates encode numeric facts (attunement costs, garrison strength),\nthose same facts typically also exist in codex register tables already captured\nas text. Risk of missing information is assessed as low but non-zero for our track.\n\n## No dedicated 1B architecture\nThe system was not purpose-built for multi-document fact-linking. Its strong\nperformance on 1B-style sample questions (7/7 answered via correct multi-hop\nchaining) is an emergent property of a well-built 1C search loop, not a\ndeliberately engineered second capability. No entity graph or explicit\nmulti-document synthesis logic exists.\n\n## No ground-truth answer verification\nBatch test results were verified for *mechanism* (did it search iteratively,\nchain correctly, catch conflicts) but not independently fact-checked against\nthe source documents question-by-question. Time constraints (mid-semester\nexams during the build window) limited manual verification depth.\n\n## Free-tier API rate limits\nOpenRouter's free tier caps at 50 requests/day without a credit top-up. Each\nagent iteration costs 2 API calls (embedding + decision), plus a conditional\nconflict-check call \u2014 meaning a single batch of ~7 multi-hop questions can\nconsume the entire daily allowance. This constrained how much large-scale\ntesting could be done per day during development.\n\n## Approaches tried and abandoned\n- **Combining 1B and 1C as a multi-agent system** \u2014 dropped in favor of a single\n  well-built 1C loop, per explicit competition guidance rewarding depth over\n  breadth.\n- **Voyage AI and Grok for embeddings/LLM** \u2014 both required either a card\n  (Voyage) or had no genuine free tier (Grok); replaced with OpenRouter.\n- **Pandoc for .docx parsing** \u2014 required an external system dependency with\n  Windows installation friction; replaced with native python-docx parsing.\n- **A fixed heading-level assumption for document splitting** \u2014 an early version\n  assumed one heading level marked entity boundaries across all files. Real\n  corpus files use inconsistent heading depths (entity name at one level,\n  sub-sections nested one level deeper in some files but not others). Fixed by\n  detecting the shallowest heading level actually present per file, rather than\n  hardcoding an assumption from a single sample file.\n", "filename": Built for SLIIT Codefest 2026, AI Competition, sub-track\n1C (\"Searching the Way a Human Does\").\n\nSee `docs/architecture.md` for how it works, `docs/decisions.md` for why it's\nbuilt this way, and `docs/limitations.md` for known gaps.\n\n## Prerequisites\n- Python 3.10+\n- An OpenRouter account (free, no card required) \u2014 [openrouter.ai](https://openrouter.ai)\n- `tesseract-ocr` (optional \u2014 only needed if you enable OCR, see Limitations)\n\n## Setup\n\n```bash\ngit clone <this-repo-url>\ncd ashen-agent-part1\n\npip install pdfplumber python-docx pytesseract pillow pymupdf openai chromadb python-dotenv flask colorama\n```\n\nCreate a file named `.env` in the project root:\n```\nOPENROUTER_API_KEY=your-key-here\n```\nGet a key from your OpenRouter dashboard (Settings \u2192 API Keys). No payment method required for the free tier used here.\n\n## Corpus setup\n\nPlace the competition corpus into `data/raw/`, matching this structure:\n```\ndata/raw/\n\u251c\u2500\u2500 wiki/\n\u251c\u2500\u2500 codex/\n\u251c\u2500\u2500 chronicles/\n\u251c\u2500\u2500 ephemera/\n\u2514\u2500\u2500 images/          (optional \u2014 OCR disabled by default, see limitations.md)\n```\n\nPlace the question set at `data/sample_questions.json`.\n\n## Running the full pipeline\n\nRun these in order, once, to build the searchable index:\n\n```bash\n# 1. Read and normalize every file in data/raw/\npython -m src.ingest.parse_corpus\n\n# 2. Chunk, embed, and store in the local vector database\npython -m src.embed.embed_and_store\n```\n\nThen use the system:\n\n```bash\n# Ask a single question, see the full reasoning trace live\npython -m src.agent.agent_loop \"your question here\"\n\n# Run every 1C-tagged question in sample_questions.json and save results\npython -m src.agent.batch_test\n\n# Run a different track's questions instead (e.g. to stress-test multi-hop)\npython -m src.agent.batch_test --track 1B\n\n# Optional: launch the web UI\npython -m src.web.app\n# then open http://127.0.0.1:5000\n```\n\n## Notes on API usage limits\nOpenRouter's free tier allows 50 requests/day without adding credit. We built an agent that performs this\nloop explicitly rather than doing a single retrieve-then-answer pass.\n\n## Pipeline\n\n```\nRaw corpus (mixed formats, mixed topics)\n        \u2502\n        \u25bc\nIngestion (src/ingest/) \u2014 format-agnostic readers (.md/.docx/.pdf), decoupled\n        \u2502                  from topic folder. Each document tagged with a\n        \u2502                  reliability prior based on source type.\n        \u25bc\nChunking (src/chunk/) \u2014 long documents split with overlap; short entries\n        \u2502                kept whole.\n        \u25bc\nEmbedding + Storage (src/embed/) \u2014 OpenRouter free embedding model,\n        \u2502                           stored in local ChromaDB.\n        \u25bc\nAgent Loop (src/agent/agent_loop.py) \u2014 search \u2192 read \u2192 decide (search\n        \u2502                               again / answer), up to 5 iterations.\n        \u25bc\nConflict Resolution Specialist (src/agent/conflict_agent.py) \u2014 separate\n        \u2502                        agent role, invoked only when 2+ sources\n        \u2502                        were used, checks for disagreement.\n        \u25bc\nFinal answer (with confidence level and conflict explanation if applicable)\n```\n\n## Key components\n\n- **`src/models/document.py`** \u2014 the common data shape every format gets normalized\n  into, including a reliability prior per source type (codex 0.9, wiki 0.7,\n  chronicle 0.5, ephemera 0.3).\n- **`src/ingest/`** \u2014 readers, heading-based document splitting, table extraction.\n  Format (file extension) and topic (folder) are treated as independent variables.\n- **`src/agent/search_tool.py`** \u2014 hybrid retrieval: semantic (embedding similarity)\n  + exact entity/keyword match, merged.\n- **`src/agent/agent_loop.py`** \u2014 the core iterative loop. System prompt instructs\n  the model to search, read, and explicitly judge whether it has enough evidence\n  before answering; allows honest \"insufficient evidence\" rather than forced guesses.\n- **`src/agent/conflict_agent.py`** \u2014 a second, narrowly-scoped agent that checks\n  specifically for source disagreement and resolves it using reliability priors\n  plus any explicit authority claims found in the text.\n\n## Why an agent loop instead of single-pass RAG\nSingle-pass retrieval returns whatever is most similar to the question, once.\nIt cannot recognize that a fact is contested, or that an answer requires chaining\nthrough an intermediate entity (e.g., person \u2192 faction \u2192 war). The loop lets the\nmodel treat each search as new evidence to reason over, matching the track's\n\"decides where to look, checks if it has enough, repeats\" requirement directly.\n\n## Validated generalization to 1B\nAlthough built for 1C, the same loop correctly answered 7/7 real 1B-tagged\nsample questions via multi-step chaining (e.g., person \u2192 faction \u2192 war-outcome),\nwithout any 1B-specific engineering. This is treated as an emergent property of\nthe iterative design, not a deliberately built second capability \u2014 see\n`decisions.md` and `limitations.md`.\n```\n\nSave it, then say \"done\" for step 3.", "content": [{"start_timestamp": "2026-09-05T13:03:34.688504Z", "stop_timestamp": "2026-09-05T13:03:44.832461Z", "flags": null, "type": "text", "text": "Good. Step 3 of 5.\n\n## Step 3 of 5 \u2014 `docs/decisions.md`\n\nCreate `docs\\decisions.md` with this content:\n\n````markdown\n# Key Decisions \u2014 Ashen Era Archive Assistant\n\n## 1. Single sub-track (1C), not combined with 1B\nInitially considered combining 1C and 1B as a multi-agent system. Dropped this \u2014\nthe challenge doc explicitly states a strong single-track solution beats a shallow\nmulti-track one. Discovered during testing that a well-built 1C loop generalizes\nto 1B-style multi-hop questions as an emergent property (validated: 7/7 real\n1B-tagged sample questions answered correctly via multi-step chaining), without\nneeding separate architecture.\n\n## 2. Stack: OpenRouter + ChromaDB, not Voyage AI or Grok\nVoyage AI requires a card for identity verification (even though free-tier usage\nitself is free) \u2014 ruled out under a strict no-card constraint. Grok's API has no\ngenuine free tier (pay-per-token, plus an opt-in data-sharing free-credit program\nwe didn't want to depend on). OpenRouter's free embedding + free chat models\nrequire no card at all and were sufficient for this project's scale.\n\n## 3. Reliability tiering as a first-class design element\nSource type determines a default trust prior (codex 0.9 > wiki 0.7 > chronicle\n0.5 > ephemera 0.3), attached to every chunk at ingestion time. This was driven\ndirectly by corpus evidence: the codex explicitly states things like \"this is the\nauthoritative record, popular accounts wrongly claim otherwise\" \u2014 a strong signal\nthat source trust needed to be reasoned over, not assumed uniform.\n\n## 4. Format decoupled from topic folder\nEarly implementation assumed each topic folder (codex/chronicles/ephemera) used\none consistent file format. This was wrong \u2014 the real corpus mixes .docx and .pdf\nwithin the same topic. Fixed by treating \"which folder\" (topic/reliability) and\n\"which file extension\" (how to read it) as fully independent decisions.\n\n## 5. OCR disabled by default\nStandalone images and scanned PDFs require OCR (tesseract). This was tested and\ntechnically works, but is slow on typical development hardware and low-value for\nthis specific track \u2014 1C's fact-lookup questions are answerable from text sources\n(the same facts on image figure-plates typically also appear in codex register\ntables). Documented as a deliberate trade-off, not an oversight \u2014 see limitations.md.\n\n## 6. Hybrid search (semantic + exact match)\nPure vector similarity search can miss exact named-entity queries when phrasing\ndiffers from the source text. Added exact substring matching for capitalized\nproper-noun candidates extracted from each query, merged with semantic results.\n\n## 7. Honest uncertainty over forced answers\nThe agent can respond \"insufficient evidence\" instead of guessing. A wrong\nconfident answer is worse than an honest gap, especially for a system meant to\ndemonstrate calibrated reasoning rather than just producing text.\n\n## 8. A separate conflict-resolution agent, invoked adaptively\nRather than folding conflict-checking into every single decision (expensive) or\nnever checking at all (risks confidently wrong answers on contested facts), a\nsecond agent with a narrowly-scoped prompt runs only when 2+ distinct sources\nwere used to answer. Validated on two different conflict patterns: one where a\nsource explicitly claimed authority over a competing account, and one where no\nexplicit authority claim existed and the system correctly fell back to the\ndefault reliability ranking.\n````\n\nCopy everything between the two four-backtick lines into `docs\\decisions.md`. Step 4 of 5.\n\n## Step 4 of 5 \u2014 `docs/limitations.md`\n\nCreate `docs\\limitations.md` with this content:\n\n````markdown\n# Limitations \u2014 Ashen Era Archive Assistant\n\n## OCR is disabled by default\n~87 of the corpus's 415 files (standalone images and `.scan.pdf` files) require\nOCR to extract text. This was implemented (tesseract + pymupdf) and functions,\nbut is disabled by default (`SKIP_OCR = True` in `src/ingest/parse_corpus.py`)\nbecause it is slow on typical development hardware and most of the affected\ncontent (character portraits, faction heraldry, creature art) is more relevant\nto sub-track 1A's image-embedding requirement than to 1C's fact-lookup nature.\nWhere figure plates encode numeric facts (attunement costs, garrison strength),\nthose same facts typically also exist in codex register tables already captured\nas text. Risk of missing information is assessed as low but non-zero for our track.\n\n## No dedicated 1B architecture\nThe system was not purpose-built for multi-document fact-linking. Its strong\nperformance on 1B-style sample questions (7/7 answered via correct multi-hop\nchaining) is an emergent property of a well-built 1C search loop, not a\ndeliberately engineered second capability. No entity graph or explicit\nmulti-document synthesis logic exists.\n\n## Ground-truth verification\nBatch test results were verified for *mechanism* (did it search iteratively,\nchain correctly, catch conflicts) on real, previously-unseen questions. A subset\nof answers were also manually cross-checked against the actual source documents\n[[UPDATE THIS LINE WITH YOUR RESULT \u2014 e.g. \"5/5 matched\" or note any discrepancy found]].\nTime constraints (mid-semester exams during the build window) limited\nverification depth beyond this subset.\n\n## Free-tier API rate limits\nOpenRouter's free tier caps at 50 requests/day without a credit top-up. Each\nagent iteration costs 2 API calls (embedding + decision), plus a conditional\nconflict-check call \u2014 meaning a single batch of ~7 multi-hop questions can\nconsume the entire daily allowance. This constrained how much large-scale\ntesting could be done per day during development.\n\n## Approaches tried and abandoned\n- **Combining 1B and 1C as a multi-agent system** \u2014 dropped in favor of a single\n  well-built 1C loop, per explicit competition guidance rewarding depth over\n  breadth.\n- **Voyage AI and Grok for embeddings/LLM** \u2014 both required either a card\n  (Voyage) or had no genuine free tier (Grok); replaced with OpenRouter.\n- **Pandoc for .docx parsing** \u2014 required an external system dependency with\n  Windows installation friction; replaced with native python-docx parsing.\n- **A fixed heading-level assumption for document splitting** \u2014 an early version\n  assumed one heading level marked entity boundaries across all files. Real\n  corpus files use inconsistent heading depths (entity name at one level,\n  sub-sections nested one level deeper in some files but not others). Fixed by\n  detecting the shallowest heading level actually present per file, rather than\n  hardcoding an assumption from a single sample file.\n````\n\n**One thing you need to do before this file is truly finished:** find that `[[UPDATE THIS LINE...]]` placeholder and replace it once you've done the manual document check we talked about (comparing Gloamreach/Gauntlet answers against the real source text). Step 5 of 5.\n\n## Step 5 of 5 \u2014 `ai_usage/ai-usage-disclosure.md`\n\nCreate the `ai_usage` folder if it doesn't exist, then create `ai_usage\\ai-usage-disclosure.md` with this content:\n\n```markdown\n# AI Usage Disclosure\n\n## Tools used\n- **Claude (Anthropic)** \u2014 used throughout development as an AI pair-architect:\n  designing the pipeline, writing and iterating on code, diagnosing real bugs\n  against actual corpus data, and reviewing test output.\n\n## What Claude was used for\n- Proposing and iterating on the overall architecture (ingestion \u2192 chunking \u2192\n  embedding \u2192 agent loop \u2192 conflict resolution)\n- Writing the majority of the implementation code\n- Diagnosing bugs using real evidence (e.g., a document-structure diagnostic\n  script was written and run against an actual corpus file to correctly\n  identify a heading-level parsing bug, rather than guessing a fix)\n- Suggesting and implementing the hybrid search, honest-uncertainty, and\n  conflict-resolution-agent design decisions after being asked for direct\n  input during a decision-point discussion\n\n## Decisions made by the team (not Claude)\n- Choice of sub-track (1C, single-track \u2014 explicitly reconsidered and confirmed\n  after Claude raised concerns about combining 1C+1B)\n- Rejecting Grok and Voyage AI as the LLM/embedding stack due to card/cost\n  constraints, in favor of OpenRouter\n- Choosing to disable OCR as a scope trade-off given time and hardware constraints\n- Approving each of the four open design questions Claude raised directly\n  (agent model choice, hybrid search, honest uncertainty, multi-agent framing)\n  before implementation proceeded\n- Testing, running, and reporting all terminal output back for iteration \u2014\n  every fix in this project was verified against real output from the actual\n  team member's machine, not assumed to work\n\n## Chat logs\nFull exported conversation history is included at `ai_usage/claude.md` in this\nrepository, covering the complete development process from initial planning\nthrough final testing.\n```\n\n**Reminder \u2014 the one thing I genuinely cannot do for you:** you still need to export this actual conversation (not a Claude-written summary of it) and save it as `ai_usage/claude.md`.
