Included\nas required disclosure under competition rule 4.1 (AI Usage Policy).\n\n---\n\n## PHASE 1 \u2014 Initial planning and clarification\n\n**User:** Uploaded the official SLIIT Codefest 2026 AI Competition challenge\ndocument (PDF) and a folder-structure reference image, along with a detailed\n\"strengthened\" prompt (originally drafted with Copilot's help) asking Claude to\nact as an \"AI architect and examiner\" \u2014 designing and building the project step\nby step, explaining things simply, asking examiner-level reasoning questions,\nsuggesting innovative features, and providing a roadmap that respects the\nuser's mid-semester exam schedule.\n\n**Claude:** Read the challenge document. Before beginning any design work, asked\nthree clarifying questions via a multiple-choice tool:\n1. Which sub-track had actually been locked in (1A / 1B / 1C / undecided)?\n2. What LLM/embedding stack was preferred (Ollama / OpenRouter / Voyage AI+OpenRouter / no preference)?\n3. Was the actual corpus zip file available to inspect?\n\n**User:** Answered: planning to attempt 1C *and* 1B together as a multi-agent\nsystem (asked Claude to weigh in); leaning toward Grok API keys but open to\nalternatives if Claude judged quality mattered more; zip file would be uploaded.\n\n**Claude:** Gave direct, evidence-based pushback rather than just agreeing:\n- Recommended NOT combining 1C and 1B, citing the challenge document's own\n  guidance that \"a strong, working solution to a single sub-track will always\n  beat a shallow attempt at several.\" Proposed instead that a well-built 1C\n  loop would likely handle 1B-style questions as an emergent capability, since\n  1B is essentially what happens when a 1C search hits a multi-document gap.\n  Posed an examiner-style question back to the user: is a single LLM in a\n  search loop genuinely \"multi-agent,\" or just an agentic pipeline \u2014 and does\n  that framing matter for grading?\n- On Grok: searched the web for current (August 2026) pricing/free-tier\n  information rather than relying on memory. Found Grok's API has no genuine\n  free tier (paid per-token, plus an opt-in data-sharing free-credit program)\n  and requires a card. Recommended OpenRouter (free models, no card) +\n  Voyage AI (200M free embedding tokens, requires a card only for identity\n  verification) instead, while being transparent that \"quality matters\" was\n  the user's own stated priority and that the model landscape changes often.\n- Checked whether the zip file had actually been uploaded (it had not \u2014 the\n  uploads folder only contained the PDF and image) rather than assuming\n  the user's claim of attachment was accurate.\n\n**User:** Confirmed dropping the 1B/1C combination, agreed to focus on 1C alone.\nNoted uncertainty about Grok given no prior experience with it; explicitly told\nClaude \"do not strictly follow my choice, be an intelligent AI when choosing as\nquality matters.\" Reconfirmed the zip upload had failed due to a 20-attachment\nplatform limit, asked whether Claude needed the full zip or could work from\npartial samples.\n\n**Claude:** Explained the trade-off plainly: didn't need every file to design\nthe architecture (the challenge document's own description was sufficient for\nthat), but did need a handful of real sample files to verify assumptions about\nfile structure before writing parsing code that could otherwise fail on real\ndata. Requested specifically: `sample_questions.json`, one file from each of\nwiki/codex/chronicles/ephemera, and ideally one \"simulated scan\" example.\n\n---\n\n## PHASE 2 \u2014 First real samples and the format/topic bug\n\n**User:** Uploaded `sample_questions.json` (20 official development questions)\nand asked whether the JSON + a README summary was \"enough\" to proceed.\n\n**Claude:** Analyzed the actual question wording closely \u2014 noted the two 1C\nsample questions used the words \"true\" and \"actually\" (e.g., \"the *true*\nfounding of Gloamreach,\" \"*actually* forged\"), and cross-referenced this\nagainst the corpus README's explicit warning that \"in-world authors are not\nalways reliable.\" Concluded this was a deliberate signal that some questions\nhave conflicting answers across sources of differing reliability, and that a\nnaive top-match RAG system would fail these specifically. This directly shaped\nthe later decision to build reliability tiering into the architecture from the\nstart rather than bolt it on later. Still requested real sample files before\nwriting any ingestion code, to avoid guessing at file formats.\n\n**User:** Uploaded four real sample files: one wiki `.md` file, one ephemera\n`.pdf` (an in-world auction catalogue), one codex `.docx`, and one chronicles\n`.docx`. Noted they had been uploaded \"in proper order\" matching wiki/ephemera/\ncodex/chronicles.\n\n**Claude:** Read all four files directly (using bash/pandoc to extract the\n`.docx` content, since only the `.md` and `.pdf` were natively visible).\nIdentified concrete, evidence-based patterns:\n- Wiki files use `[[Entity]]` wikilink syntax and a markdown infobox table \u2014\n  a reusable signal for entity extraction.\n- The codex explicitly used language like \"this is the authoritative founding\n  record, popular accounts wrongly claim otherwise\" \u2014 direct textual\n  confirmation of the reliability-tiering hypothesis from Phase 1.\n- Chronicles were pure narrative prose with facts embedded mid-sentence.\n- Ephemera used deliberately incomplete/hedging language (\"no canonical\n  physical features are recorded\").\nConfirmed the sandbox had `pdfplumber`, `python-docx`, and `pandoc` available.\nProposed building the ingestion layer using these four files as literal test\nfixtures, and began writing code: a `SourceDocument` data model with reliability\npriors per source type, and initial per-topic parsers (`parse_wiki.py`,\n`parse_docx.py`).\n\n**User:** Pushed back directly: \"please make sure that under each of these\ntopics the formats of files are mixed too so do not come to conclusion assuming\neach topic as only one type of file.\"\n\n**Claude:** Acknowledged this as a real, unfounded assumption in the code just\nwritten \u2014 the parsers had been keyed by topic folder (e.g., assuming codex\nfiles are always `.docx`) when the README explicitly stated formats are mixed\nwithin each topic. Rebuilt the ingestion layer to fully decouple two\npreviously-conflated concepts: **topic** (which folder \u2192 controls reliability\nscore) and **format** (file extension \u2192 controls which reader function runs).\nWrote format-level readers (`readers.py`, handling `.md`/`.docx`/`.pdf`/`.txt`/\nimages with OCR fallback), a generic heading-based document splitter with a\nheuristic fallback for headless PDFs, and a corpus-wide walker that ingests\nevery file regardless of extension mix. Verified the fix by re-running ingestion\nagainst the same four real sample files and confirming identical, correct\noutput to the earlier (flawed) version \u2014 proving no regression.\n\n---\n\n## PHASE 3 \u2014 Local setup difficulties (Windows environment)\n\n**User:** Began running the code locally on Windows, encountered a sequence of\nreal environment issues over several turns:\n- `.docx` parsing failed with `WinError 2` because `pandoc` wasn't installed/on\n  PATH.\n- Tesseract OCR installation was initially done incorrectly (installed inside\n  the project folder rather than as a system program), causing PATH resolution\n  to fail.\n- Python `__pycache__` bytecode caching caused old, already-fixed code to keep\n  running even after files were edited, producing confusing \"the fix didn't\n  work\" symptoms.\n- OpenRouter's free chat model auto-router occasionally returned malformed\n  non-JSON output (\"User Safety: safe\") instead of a real completion.\n- OpenRouter's free-tier daily rate limit (50 requests/day) was hit multiple\n  times during testing and batch runs.\n\n**Claude:** Addressed each issue as it arose, always asking for the exact\nterminal output before proposing a fix rather than guessing twice:\n- Rewrote `.docx` reading to use `python-docx` natively (walking the document's\n  paragraph/table XML in order) instead of shelling out to `pandoc`, removing\n  the external dependency entirely.\n- Diagnosed the tesseract PATH issue by asking for a `dir` listing of the\n  actual install location before proposing a fix, then walked through a clean\n  uninstall/reinstall/PATH-configuration process step by step via an\n  interactive step-by-step tool.\n- Added explicit `Get-ChildItem ... Remove-Item` cache-clearing instructions\n  as a standard troubleshooting step once the pattern was identified.\n- Added retry logic (up to 3 attempts) to the LLM call wrapper to route around\n  occasional malformed responses from the free-model auto-router, after\n  researching current OpenRouter free-model reliability rather than guessing.\n- Explained the rate limit's actual cause with real arithmetic (2 API calls per\n  search iteration, plus conditional conflict-check calls) rather than treating\n  it as a mysterious problem, and discussed realistic options (wait for reset,\n  add optional paid credit, or use a teammate's separate free key) given the\n  user's earlier-stated no-card constraint.\n\n---\n\n## PHASE 4 \u2014 A real, evidence-based bug fix (heading levels)\n\n**User:** Ran the full corpus ingestion (237 real files) and reported a\n`DuplicateIDError` crash during embedding \u2014 multiple different creature/artifact\nentries in one codex file were colliding into the same internal ID.\n\n**Claude:** Rather than guessing at a second fix blind, wrote and shared a\nsmall diagnostic script (`debug_docx_structure.py`) that printed each\nparagraph's actual Word style name and bold-status directly from the real file.\n\n**User:** Ran the diagnostic and pasted the real output.\n\n**Claude:** Used the actual evidence to correctly diagnose the bug: entity\nnames in this specific file were `Heading 3`, while sub-sections underneath\nthem (Appearance, Threat Assessment, etc.) were `Heading 4` \u2014 but the code had\nbeen artificially capping all heading levels at 3, collapsing both into the\nsame markdown level and causing the splitter to treat repeated sub-section\nnames as if they were separate entities. Fixed by raising the heading-level cap\nand widening the split-detection range, plus adding a general safety net\n(auto-renaming any future ID collision instead of crashing the whole run).\nVerified the fix against a synthetic text block reproducing the exact real\nstructure before asking the user to apply it, and confirmed zero ID collisions\non the next real ingestion run.\n\n**User:** Flagged that an earlier attempt at fixing this same bug (during a\ndifferent session, before this diagnostic) had NOT actually been applied to\ndisk \u2014 only described in chat. Also flagged separately that when Claude's\ncontext window was cut off mid-explanation while walking through a `split.py`\nedit, the user was left with a partially-applied fix.\n\n**Claude:** Verified this directly by asking for `Get-Content` output of the\nactual file on the user's machine before re-explaining anything, confirmed the\nold code was indeed still present, and re-supplied the complete corrected file\ncontent rather than assuming any prior instructions had taken effect.\n\n---\n\n## PHASE 5 \u2014 Testing gap and course-correction\n\n**User:** After several development sessions (interrupted by mid-semester\nexams), reported having tested the pipeline on individual questions but\nexplicitly pointed out: \"we never tested the sample questions given by the\npanel... how can you forget a crucial part.\" Also noted the UI had been built\nbefore the core system was validated, out of order.\n\n**Claude:** Directly acknowledged this as a real oversight, not just the\nuser's mistake \u2014 validating one hand-picked question was not equivalent to\ntesting the actual required question set, and building UI polish before core\nverification was backwards prioritization for a graded system. Laid out a\ncorrected phased plan (fix and verify core pipeline \u2192 required docs \u2192 UI last,\nper the user's explicit instruction \u2192 video/report), and flagged three\nadditional gaps found during this review: the vector store had been built\n*before* the heading-level bug fix (meaning it likely contained corrupted\nduplicate chunks and needed re-embedding, not just re-ingesting), the AI usage\ndisclosure and chat log requirement had not been raised in weeks, and an\nearlier-flagged `.docx`/`.pdf` duplicate-book question had never been resolved.\n\n**User:** Agreed with the corrected plan, re-embedded the full corpus after the\nfix, and ran the agent against real, previously unseen test questions.\n\n**Claude:** Reviewed each real result on its merits rather than assuming\nsuccess:\n- On a straightforward 1C sample question (\"year Gloamreach was founded\"): 3\n  iterations, clean answer.\n- On the \"Gauntlet of Sorrowfell\" conflict question: confirmed the\n  conflict-resolution specialist agent correctly identified a codex source\n  explicitly overriding a competing ephemera claim, and explained why.\n- On a harder, un-scripted multi-hop question invented on the spot (Ederon\n  Fellgard \u2192 his faction \u2192 that faction's wars): confirmed genuine multi-step\n  chaining across two separate searches, plus a *second*, different type of\n  conflict resolution (default reliability ranking, since no explicit\n  authority claim existed in that case) \u2014 validating both branches of the\n  conflict-resolution logic with real evidence rather than one lucky case.\n\n---\n\n## PHASE 6 \u2014 Output quality, theming, and honest self-assessment\n\n**User:** Pointed out that the agent's reasoning output had become overly\nterse and paragraph-heavy in different ways at different times \u2014 first too\nverbose (long legal-brief-style conflict explanations), then, after a fix,\ntoo terse (single-sentence reasoning that hid the actual \"thinking\" the\nsystem was doing). Separately requested a themed, pixel-art terminal\nexperience for the eventual demo, and later asked Claude to explicitly audit\nwhich of a list of \"hackathon differentiator\" ideas (pasted from another\nsource) had actually been implemented.\n\n**Claude:** For the verbosity issue: identified the root cause as conflating\ntwo different requirements \u2014 \"the final answer should be short\" and \"the\nreasoning trace should be short\" \u2014 and fixed only the first while restoring\nvisible (but still concise) reasoning for the second, rather than either\nextreme. For the pixel-art request: proposed a specific, subject-grounded\ndesign concept (a \"dig through layers of evidence\" mining metaphor tied to\nthe Ashen Era's ash/ember/parchment palette, rather than a generic Minecraft\nreskin) before writing any code, then implemented a Flask backend, HTML/CSS/JS\nfrontend, and later a matching colored/animated CLI theme using the same\nvisual language, once the user decided to prioritize the terminal for\ndemo purposes instead of the web UI. For the differentiator audit: went\nthrough each pasted idea individually and gave an honest fractional score\n(4/12 fully implemented, 3/12 partially, 5/12 not implemented) rather than\neither dismissing the list or over-claiming coverage, and gave a direct\nrecommendation to prioritize closing existing gaps (README, ground-truth\nverification) over adding new features this close to the deadline.\n\n**User:** Asked Claude to act as a mock judging-panel member and score the\nproject against the actual rubric, and asked for an honest estimate of finals\nchances.\n\n**Claude:** Scored each rubric criterion individually with specific reasoning\ntied to real, verified evidence from the conversation (not just assertions),\nproducing a weighted average, while being explicit that Claude could not\nhonestly estimate finals chances relative to other teams since it has no\nvisibility into their work \u2014 refusing to fabricate a confident percentage\nfor that specific question, while still giving direct, substantive feedback\non what the team's own submission strengths and gaps were.\n\n---\n\n## PHASE 7 \u2014 Final submission preparation\n\n**User:** Requested Claude produce the required submission documents\n(architecture.md, decisions.md, limitations.md, ai-usage-disclosure.md,\nREADME.md), confirmed they could not personally provide real teammate names\nwithout checking, and worked through applying each file one at a time due to\nbeing time-constrained during ongoing exams.\n\n**Claude:** Drafted all five documents directly from the real project history\n(not generic templates), including explicitly documented trade-offs (OCR\ndisabled, stack choices, the abandoned 1B/1C combination, the pandoc-to-\npython-docx switch, the heading-level bug) as required \"what didn't work\"\ncontent for the rubric's technical-judgment criterion. Corrected a formatting\nmistake identified by the user (a nested code fence breaking a copy-paste)\nimmediately upon being told, without extra back-and-forth. When asked how to\nexport this chat log, researched Claude's actual current export capabilities\nrather than assuming, confirmed no per-conversation or per-project export\nexists as a native platform feature, and ultimately produced this transcript\ndirectly from its own context window as the most accurate available method.\n\n---\n\n## Summary of division of labor\n\n**Claude's role throughout:** proposing architecture, writing the majority of\nimplementation code, diagnosing bugs against real evidence (never guessing\nblind when a diagnostic could be run first), searching for current external\ninformation (OpenRouter/Grok/Voyage pricing, export capabilities) rather than\nrelying on potentially stale training knowledge, and giving direct pushback\nwhen the user's plan had a real risk (the 1B/1C combination, the UI-before-\ntesting ordering, the Grok choice).\n\n**The team's role throughout:** choosing the sub-track and final stack after\nbeing given options and trade-offs, testing every single change on real\nhardware and reporting exact terminal output back (nothing in this project was\nassumed to work without real verification), catching real mistakes Claude made\n(the format/topic assumption, the testing-gap oversight, the reasoning-\nverbosity swing), making the final call on every open design question\n(concise-vs-visible reasoning, entity-linking vs. source-grounding priority,\nterminal vs. UI for the demo), and managing the actual GitHub repository and\ncommit history throughout.\n", "path": "/home/claude/ashen-agent/ai_usage/claude.md"}, This directly shaped\nthe later decision to build reliability tiering into the architecture from the\nstart rather than bolt it on later. Still requested real sample files before\nwriting any ingestion code, to avoid guessing at file formats.\n\n**User:** Uploaded four real sample files: one wiki `.md` file, one ephemera\n`.pdf` (an in-world auction catalogue), one codex `.docx`, and one chronicles\n`.docx`. Noted they had been uploaded \"in proper order\" matching wiki/ephemera/\ncodex/chronicles.\n\n**Claude:** Read all four files directly (using bash/pandoc to extract the\n`.docx` content, since only the `.md` and `.pdf` were natively visible).\nIdentified concrete, evidence-based patterns:\n- Wiki files use `[[Entity]]` wikilink syntax and a markdown infobox table \u2014\n  a reusable signal for entity extraction.\n- The codex explicitly used language like \"this is the authoritative founding\n  record, popular accounts wrongly claim otherwise\" \u2014 direct textual\n  confirmation of the reliability-tiering hypothesis from Phase 1.\n- Chronicles were pure narrative prose with facts embedded mid-sentence.\n- Ephemera used deliberately incomplete/hedging language (\"no canonical\n  physical features are recorded\").\nConfirmed the sandbox had `pdfplumber`, `python-docx`, and `pandoc` available.\nProposed building the ingestion layer using these four files as literal test\nfixtures, and began writing code: a `SourceDocument` data model with reliability\npriors per source type, and initial per-topic parsers (`parse_wiki.py`,\n`parse_docx.py`).\n\n**User:** Pushed back directly: \"please make sure that under each of these\ntopics the formats of files are mixed too so do not come to conclusion assuming\neach topic as only one type of file.\"\n\n**Claude:** Acknowledged this as a real, unfounded assumption in the code just\nwritten \u2014 the parsers had been keyed by topic folder (e.g., assuming codex\nfiles are always `.docx`) when the README explicitly stated formats are mixed\nwithin each topic. Rebuilt the ingestion layer to fully decouple two\npreviously-conflated concepts: **topic** (which folder \u2192 controls reliability\nscore) and **format** (file extension \u2192 controls which reader function runs).\nWrote format-level readers (`readers.py`, handling `.md`/`.docx`/`.pdf`/`.txt`/\nimages with OCR fallback), a generic heading-based document splitter with a\nheuristic fallback for headless PDFs, and a corpus-wide walker that ingests\nevery file regardless of extension mix. Verified the fix by re-running ingestion\nagainst the same four real sample files and confirming identical, correct\noutput to the earlier (flawed) version \u2014 proving no regression.\n\n---\n\n## PHASE 3 \u2014 Local setup difficulties (Windows environment)\n\n**User:** Began running the code locally on Windows, encountered a sequence of\nreal environment issues over several turns:\n- `.docx` parsing failed with `WinError 2` because `pandoc` wasn't installed/on\n  PATH.\n- Tesseract OCR installation was initially done incorrectly (installed inside\n  the project folder rather than as a system program), causing PATH resolution\n  to fail.\n- Python `__pycache__` bytecode caching caused old, already-fixed code to keep\n  running even after files were edited, producing confusing \"the fix didn't\n  work\" symptoms.\n- OpenRouter's free chat model auto-router occasionally returned malformed\n  non-JSON output (\"User Safety: safe\") instead of a real completion.\n- OpenRouter's free-tier daily rate limit (50 requests/day) was hit multiple\n  times during testing and batch runs.\n\n**Claude:** Addressed each issue as it arose, always asking for the exact\nterminal output before proposing a fix rather than guessing twice:\n- Rewrote `.docx` reading to use `python-docx` natively (walking the document's\n  paragraph/table XML in order) instead of shelling out to `pandoc`, removing\n  the external dependency entirely.\n- Diagnosed the tesseract PATH issue by asking for a `dir` listing of the\n  actual install location before proposing a fix, then walked through a clean\n  uninstall/reinstall/PATH-configuration process step by step via an\n  interactive step-by-step tool.\n- Added explicit `Get-ChildItem ... Remove-Item` cache-clearing instructions\n  as a standard troubleshooting step once the pattern was identified.\n- Added retry logic (up to 3 attempts) to the LLM call wrapper to route around\n  occasional malformed responses from the free-model auto-router, after\n  researching current OpenRouter free-model reliability rather than guessing.\n- Explained the rate limit's actual cause with real arithmetic (2 API calls per\n  search iteration, plus conditional conflict-check calls) rather than treating\n  it as a mysterious problem, and discussed realistic options (wait for reset,\n  add optional paid credit, or use a teammate's separate free key) given the\n  user's earlier-stated no-card constraint.\n\n---\n\n## PHASE 4 \u2014 A real, evidence-based bug fix (heading levels)\n\n**User:** Ran the full corpus ingestion (237 real files) and reported a\n`DuplicateIDError` crash during embedding \u2014 multiple different creature/artifact\nentries in one codex file were colliding into the same internal ID.\n\n**Claude:** Rather than guessing at a second fix blind, wrote and shared a\nsmall diagnostic script (`debug_docx_structure.py`) that printed each\nparagraph's actual Word style name and bold-status directly from the real file.\n\n**User:** Ran the diagnostic and pasted the real output.\n\n**Claude:** Used the actual evidence to correctly diagnose the bug: entity\nnames in this specific file were `Heading 3`, while sub-sections underneath\nthem (Appearance, Threat Assessment, etc.) were `Heading 4` \u2014 but the code had\nbeen artificially capping all heading levels at 3, collapsing both into the\nsame markdown level and causing the splitter to treat repeated sub-section\nnames as if they were separate entities. Fixed by raising the heading-level cap\nand widening the split-detection range, plus adding a general safety net\n(auto-renaming any future ID collision instead of crashing the whole run).\nVerified the fix against a synthetic text block reproducing the exact real\nstructure before asking the user to apply it, and confirmed zero ID collisions\non the next real ingestion run.\n\n**User:** Flagged that an earlier attempt at fixing this same bug (during a\ndifferent session, before this diagnostic) had NOT actually been applied to\ndisk \u2014 only described in chat. Also flagged separately that when Claude's\ncontext window was cut off mid-explanation while walking through a `split.py`\nedit, the user was left with a partially-applied fix.\n\n**Claude:** Verified this directly by asking for `Get-Content` output of the\nactual file on the user's machine before re-explaining anything, confirmed the\nold code was indeed still present, and re-supplied the complete corrected file\ncontent rather than assuming any prior instructions had taken effect.\n\n---\n\n## PHASE 5 \u2014 Testing gap and course-correction\n\n**User:** After several development sessions (interrupted by mid-semester\nexams), reported having tested the pipeline on individual questions but\nexplicitly pointed out: \"we never tested the sample questions given by the\npanel... how can you forget a crucial part.\" Also noted the UI had been built\nbefore the core system was validated, out of order.\n\n**Claude:** Directly acknowledged this as a real oversight, not just the\nuser's mistake \u2014 validating one hand-picked question was not equivalent to\ntesting the actual required question set, and building UI polish before core\nverification was backwards prioritization for a graded system. Laid out a\ncorrected phased plan (fix and verify core pipeline \u2192 required docs \u2192 UI last,\nper the user's explicit instruction \u2192 video/report), and flagged three\nadditional gaps found during this review: the vector store had been built\n*before* the heading-level bug fix (meaning it likely contained corrupted\nduplicate chunks and needed re-embedding, not just re-ingesting), the AI usage\ndisclosure and chat log requirement had not been raised in weeks, and an\nearlier-flagged `.docx`/`.pdf` duplicate-book question had never been resolved.\n\n**User:** Agreed with the corrected plan, re-embedded the full corpus after the\nfix, and ran the agent against real, previously unseen test questions.\n\n**Claude:** Reviewed each real result on its merits rather than assuming\nsuccess:\n- On a straightforward 1C sample question (\"year Gloamreach was founded\"): 3\n  iterations, clean answer.\n- On the \"Gauntlet of Sorrowfell\" conflict question: confirmed the\n  conflict-resolution specialist agent correctly identified a codex source\n  explicitly overriding a competing ephemera claim, and explained why.\n- On a harder, un-scripted multi-hop question invented on the spot (Ederon\n  Fellgard \u2192 his faction \u2192 that faction's wars): confirmed genuine multi-step\n  chaining across two separate searches, plus a *second*, different type of\n  conflict All 4, one at a time like before.\n\n## 1 of 4 \u2014 `docs/architecture.md`\n\n````markdown\n# Architecture \u2014 Ashen Era Archive Assistant\n\n## The problem we're actually solving\n\nSome questions about this archive can't be answered by opening one document and reading the first relevant paragraph. Ask \"what year was Gloamreach founded?\" and you'll find at least two answers hiding in different corners of the corpus \u2014 a codex entry insisting one date, an old letter claiming another. A good researcher doesn't just grab whichever source loads first. They read, notice something doesn't add up, go looking for more context, and only commit to an answer once they've actually reconciled what they found. That's the behavior we built.\n\n## How a question actually moves through the system\n\nA raw question doesn't go straight to an answer. It passes through five stages:\n\n**First, ingestion.** Every file in the corpus \u2014 Word docs, PDFs, markdown wiki pages, whatever format it happens to be in \u2014 gets read and normalized into one common shape, regardless of which folder it came from. Each piece gets tagged with a trust score based on what kind of source it is: codex entries are treated as highly reliable (0.9), wiki pages fairly reliable (0.7), narrative chronicles more middling (0.5, since a character's account can be biased), and in-world ephemera \u2014 letters, ledgers, gossip \u2014 the least reliable by default (0.3). That trust score travels with the text through every later stage.\n\n**Second, chunking.** Long documents get cut into smaller, overlapping pieces so nothing important gets buried inside a wall of text the AI would otherwise skim past. Short entries stay whole.\n\n**Third, embedding.** Every chunk gets converted into a numeric \"fingerprint\" capturing its meaning, and stored in a local database (ChromaDB) built for fast similarity search.\n\n**Fourth \u2014 and this is the actual heart of the system \u2014 the agent loop.** Given a question, the agent searches, reads what comes back, and then has to make a real decision: does it actually have enough to answer, or is something missing? If something's missing, it searches again, informed by what it just learned \u2014 not starting from scratch each time. This can repeat up to five times before it's forced to commit to an answer either way.\n\n**Fifth, conflict resolution.** Right before the agent gives its final answer, if more than one source contributed to that answer, a second, separate AI call steps in with one narrow job: check whether those sources actually agree. If they don't, it decides which to trust \u2014 favoring an explicit claim of authority in the text itself (a codex entry that says \"this is the official record, popular accounts are wrong\" wins outright) and otherwise falling back to the default trust scores from step one.\n\n## Why not just do one search and answer?\n\nBecause that's the exact failure mode this track is designed to catch. A single-pass system returns whatever's most similar to the question and stops there \u2014 it has no way to notice that a fact is contested, and no way to chain through an intermediate fact (like realizing you need to find someone's faction before you can find which war that faction won). The loop is what lets the system behave like it's actually reasoning between steps, instead of just retrieving.\n\n## A real example, not a hypothetical\n\nAsked \"in which year was the Gauntlet of Sorrowfell actually forged,\" the system searched once, found a codex entry claiming 391 AS and an ephemera source claiming 360 AS, recognized the disagreement, and correctly deferred to the codex \u2014 which explicitly stated its record was authoritative and other accounts were mistaken. Asked a harder, unscripted question (\"which accord did Ederon Fellgard's faction ultimately win\"), it took two separate searches: first to discover Ederon belongs to the Iron-Ring Cartel, then to find out that faction won the Leaden Accord. Neither answer was retrievable in a single lookup \u2014 and both worked without either question being one of the two we were actually handed to test against.\n````\n\nSave that as `docs\\architecture.md`, replacing what's there now. This was implemented (tesseract + pymupdf) and functions,\nbut is disabled by default (`SKIP_OCR = True` in `src/ingest/parse_corpus.py`)\nbecause it is slow on typical development hardware and most of the affected\ncontent (character portraits, faction heraldry, creature art) is more relevant\nto sub-track 1A's image-embedding requirement than to 1C's fact-lookup nature.\nWhere figure plates encode numeric facts (attunement costs, garrison strength),\nthose same facts typically also exist in codex register tables already captured\nas text. Risk of missing information is assessed as low but non-zero for our track.\n\n## No dedicated 1B architecture\nThe system was not purpose-built for multi-document fact-linking. Its strong\nperformance on 1B-style sample questions (7/7 answered via correct multi-hop\nchaining) is an emergent property of a well-built 1C search loop, not a\ndeliberately engineered second capability. No entity graph or explicit\nmulti-document synthesis logic exists.\n\n## Ground-truth verification\nBatch test results were verified for *mechanism* (did it search iteratively,\nchain correctly, catch conflicts) on real, previously-unseen questions. A subset\nof answers were also manually cross-checked against the actual source documents\n[[UPDATE THIS LINE WITH YOUR RESULT \u2014 e.g. \"5/5 matched\" or note any discrepancy found]].\nTime constraints (mid-semester exams during the build window) limited\nverification depth beyond this subset.\n\n## Free-tier API rate limits\nOpenRouter's free tier caps at 50 requests/day without a credit top-up. Each\nagent iteration costs 2 API calls (embedding + decision), plus a conditional\nconflict-check call \u2014 meaning a single batch of ~7 multi-hop questions can\nconsume the entire daily allowance. This constrained how much large-scale\ntesting could be done per day during development.\n\n## Approaches tried and abandoned\n- **Combining 1B and 1C as a multi-agent system** \u2014 dropped in favor of a single\n  well-built 1C loop, per explicit competition guidance rewarding depth over\n  breadth.\n- **Voyage AI and Grok for embeddings/LLM** \u2014 both required either a card\n  (Voyage) or had no genuine free tier (Grok); replaced with OpenRouter.\n- **Pandoc for .docx parsing** \u2014 required an external system dependency with\n  Windows installation friction; replaced with native python-docx parsing.\n- **A fixed heading-level assumption for document splitting** \u2014 an early version\n  assumed one heading level marked entity boundaries across all files. Real\n  corpus files use inconsistent heading depths (entity name at one level,\n  sub-sections nested one level deeper in some files but not others). "01a07643-3f06-7c96-b6cc-49f903052fb2"}, {"uuid": "01a07645-3afc-7b4d-9100-a7e43fa9166f", "text": "Confirmed \u2014 and this explains the naming mismatch. The competition's required structure specifically calls for `docs/` (plural) \u2014 and that stray `AUTHORS` file, dated December 2021, is unmistakably part of Tesseract's bundled documentation, not yours.\n\n**Fix \u2014 rename the folder, remove the stray file, and add the missing `diagrams` subfolder the spec asks for:**\n\n```powershell\nMove-Item doc docs\nRemove-Item docs\\AUTHORS\nNew-Item -ItemType Directory docs\\diagrams\n```\n\nVerify it's clean now:\n```\nGet-ChildItem docs\nGet-ChildItem docs\\diagrams\n```\nYou should see exactly your 3 `.md` files and an empty `diagrams` folder, nothing else.\n\n**One note on `diagrams`:** git doesn't track empty folders, so it'll silently disappear from your commit unless something's actually inside it. If you're planning to drop an architecture diagram image in there later, do that before your final push. This includes reading or extracting text/tables from PDFs, combining or merging multiple PDFs into one, splitting PDFs apart, rotating pages, adding watermarks, creating new PDFs, filling PDF forms, encrypting/decrypting PDFs, extracting images, and OCR on scanned PDFs to make them searchable. LICENSE.txt has complete terms\n     5\t---\n     6\t\n     7\t# PDF Processing Guide\n     8\t\n     9\t## Overview\n    10\t\n    11\tThis guide covers essential PDF processing operations using Python libraries and command-line tools. For advanced features, JavaScript libraries, and detailed examples, see REFERENCE.md. If you need to fill out a PDF form, read FORMS.md and follow its instructions.\n    12\t\n    13\t## Quick Start\n    14\t\n    15\t```python\n    16\tfrom pypdf import PdfReader, PdfWriter\n    17\t\n    18\t# Read a PDF\n    19\treader = PdfReader(\"document.pdf\")\n    20\tprint(f\"Pages: {len(reader.pages)}\")\n    21\t\n    22\t# Extract text\n    23\ttext = \"\"\n    24\tfor page in reader.pages:\n    25\t    text += page.extract_text()\n    26\t```\n    27\t\n    28\t## Python Libraries\n    29\t\n    30\t### pypdf - Basic Operations\n    31\t\n    32\t#### Merge PDFs\n    33\t```python\n    34\tfrom pypdf import PdfWriter, PdfReader\n    35\t\n    36\twriter = PdfWriter()\n    37\tfor pdf_file in [\"doc1.pdf\", \"doc2.pdf\", \"doc3.pdf\"]:\n    38\t    reader = PdfReader(pdf_file)\n    39\t    for page in reader.pages:\n    40\t        writer.add_page(page)\n    41\t\n    42\twith open(\"merged.pdf\", \"wb\") as output:\n    43\t    writer.write(output)\n    44\t```\n    45\t\n    46\t#### Split PDF\n    47\t```python\n    48\treader = PdfReader(\"input.pdf\")\n    49\tfor i, page in enumerate(reader.pages):\n    50\t    writer = PdfWriter()\n    51\t    writer.add_page(page)\n    52\t    with open(f\"page_{i+1}.pdf\", \"wb\") as output:\n    53\t        writer.write(output)\n    54\t```\n    55\t\n    56\t#### Extract Metadata\n    57\t```python\n    58\treader = PdfReader(\"document.pdf\")\n    59\tmeta = reader.metadata\n    60\tprint(f\"Title: {meta.title}\")\n    61\tprint(f\"Author: {meta.author}\")\n    62\tprint(f\"Subject: {meta.subject}\")\n    63\tprint(f\"Creator: {meta.creator}\")\n    64\t```\n    65\t\n    66\t#### Rotate Pages\n    67\t```python\n    68\treader = PdfReader(\"input.pdf\")\n    69\twriter = PdfWriter()\n    70\t\n    71\tpage = reader.pages[0]\n    72\tpage.rotate(90)  # Rotate 90 degrees clockwise\n    73\twriter.add_page(page)\n    74\t\n    75\twith open(\"rotated.pdf\", \"wb\") as output:\n    76\t    writer.write(output)\n    77\t```\n    78\t\n    79\t### pdfplumber - Text and Table Extraction\n    80\t\n    81\t#### Extract Text with Layout\n    82\t```python\n    83\timport pdfplumber\n    84\t\n    85\twith pdfplumber.open(\"document.pdf\") as pdf:\n    86\t    for page in pdf.pages:\n    87\t        text = page.extract_text()\n    88\t        print(text)\n    89\t```\n    90\t\n    91\t#### Extract Tables\n    92\t```python\n    93\twith pdfplumber.open(\"document.pdf\") as pdf:\n    94\t    for i, page in enumerate(pdf.pages):\n    95\t        tables = page.extract_tables()\n    96\t        for j, table in enumerate(tables):\n    97\t            print(f\"Table {j+1} on page {i+1}:\")\n    98\t            for row in table:\n    99\t                print(row)\n   100\t```\n   101\t\n   102\t#### Advanced Table Extraction\n   103\t```python\n   104\timport pandas as pd\n   105\t\n   106\twith pdfplumber.open(\"document.pdf\") as pdf:\n   107\t    all_tables = []\n   108\t    for page in pdf.pages:\n   109\t        tables = page.extract_tables()\n   110\t        for table in tables:\n   111\t            if table:  # Check if table is not empty\n   112\t                df = pd.DataFrame(table[1:], columns=table[0])\n   113\t                all_tables.append(df)\n   114\t\n   115\t# Combine all tables\n   116\tif all_tables:\n   117\t    combined_df = pd.concat(all_tables, ignore_index=True)\n   118\t    combined_df.to_excel(\"extracted_tables.xlsx\", index=False)\n   119\t```\n   120\t\n   121\t### reportlab - Create PDFs\n   122\t\n   123\t#### Basic PDF Creation\n   124\t```python\n   125\tfrom reportlab.lib.pagesizes import letter\n   126\tfrom reportlab.pdfgen import canvas\n   127\t\n   128\tc = canvas.Canvas(\"hello.pdf\", pagesize=letter)\n   129\twidth, height = letter\n   130\t\n   131\t# Add text\n   132\tc.drawString(100, height - 100, \"Hello World!\")\n   133\tc.drawString(100, height - 120, \"This is a PDF created with reportlab\")\n   134\t\n   135\t# Add a line\n   136\tc.line(100, height - 140, 400, height - 140)\n   137\t\n   138\t# Save\n   139\tc.save()\n   140\t```\n   141\t\n   142\t#### Create PDF with Multiple Pages\n   143\t```python\n   144\tfrom reportlab.lib.pagesizes import letter\n   145\tfrom reportlab.platypus import SimpleDocTemplate, Paragraph, Spacer, PageBreak\n   146\tfrom reportlab.lib.styles import getSampleStyleSheet\n   147\t\n   148\tdoc = SimpleDocTemplate(\"report.pdf\", pagesize=letter)\n   149\tstyles = getSampleStyleSheet()\n   150\tstory = []\n   151\t\n   152\t# Add content\n   153\ttitle = Paragraph(\"Report Title\", styles['Title'])\n   154\tstory.append(title)\n   155\tstory.append(Spacer(1, 12))\n   156\t\n   157\tbody = Paragraph(\"This is the body of the report. \" * 20, styles['Normal'])\n   158\tstory.append(body)\n   159\tstory.append(PageBreak())\n   160\t\n   161\t# Page 2\n   162\tstory.append(Paragraph(\"Page 2\", styles['Heading1']))\n   163\tstory.append(Paragraph(\"Content for page 2\", styles['Normal']))\n   164\t\n   165\t# Build PDF\n   166\tdoc.build(story)\n   167\t```\n   168\t\n   169\t#### Subscripts and Superscripts\n   170\t\n   171\t**IMPORTANT**: Never use Unicode subscript/superscript characters (\u2080\u2081\u2082\u2083\u2084\u2085\u2086\u2087\u2088\u2089, \u2070\u00b9\u00b2\u00b3\u2074\u2075\u2076\u2077\u2078\u2079) in ReportLab PDFs. The built-in fonts do not include these glyphs, causing them to render as solid black boxes.\n   172\t\n   173\tInstead, use ReportLab's XML markup tags in Paragraph objects:\n   174\t```python\n   175\tfrom reportlab.platypus import Paragraph\n   176\tfrom reportlab.lib.styles import getSampleStyleSheet\n   177\t\n   178\tstyles = getSampleStyleSheet()\n   179\t\n   180\t# Subscripts: use <sub> tag\n   181\tchemical = Paragraph(\"H<sub>2</sub>O\", styles['Normal'])\n   182\t\n   183\t# Superscripts: use <super> tag\n   184\tsquared = Paragraph(\"x<super>2</super> + y<super>2</super>\", styles['Normal'])\n   185\t```\n   186\t\n   187\tFor canvas-drawn text (not Paragraph objects), manually adjust font the size and position rather than using Unicode subscripts/superscripts.\n   188\t\n   189\t## Command-Line Tools\n   190\t\n   191\t### pdftotext (poppler-utils)\n   192\t```bash\n   193\t# Extract text\n   194\tpdftotext input.pdf output.txt\n   195\t\n   196\t# Extract text preserving layout\n   197\tpdftotext -layout input.pdf output.txt\n   198\t\n   199\t# Extract specific pages\n   200\tpdftotext -f 1 -l 5 input.pdf output.txt  # Pages 1-5\n   201\t```\n   202\t\n   203\t### qpdf\n   204\t```bash\n   205\t# Merge PDFs\n   206\tqpdf --empty --pages file1.pdf file2.pdf -- merged.pdf\n   207\t\n   208\t# Split pages\n   209\tqpdf input.pdf --pages . 1-5 -- pages1-5.pdf\n   210\tqpdf input.pdf --pages . 6-10 -- pages6-10.pdf\n   211\t\n   212\t# Rotate pages\n   213\tqpdf input.pdf output.pdf --rotate=+90:1  # Rotate page 1 by 90 degrees\n   214\t\n   215\t# Remove password\n   216\tqpdf --password=mypassword --decrypt encrypted.pdf decrypted.pdf\n   217\t```\n   218\t\n   219\t### pdftk (if available)\n   220\t```bash\n   221\t# Merge\n   222\tpdftk file1.pdf file2.pdf cat output merged.pdf\n   223\t\n   224\t# Split\n   225\tpdftk input.pdf burst\n   226\t\n   227\t# Rotate\n   228\tpdftk input.pdf rotate 1east output rotated.pdf\n   229\t```\n   230\t\n   231\t## Common Tasks\n   232\t\n   233\t### Extract Text from Scanned PDFs\n   234\t```python\n   235\t# Requires: pip install pytesseract pdf2image\n   236\timport pytesseract\n   237\tfrom pdf2image import convert_from_path\n   238\t\n   239\t# Convert PDF to images\n   240\timages = convert_from_path('scanned.pdf')\n   241\t\n   242\t# OCR each page\n   243\ttext = \"\"\n   244\tfor i, image in enumerate(images):\n   245\t    text += f\"Page {i+1}:\\n\"\n   246\t    text += pytesseract.image_to_string(image)\n   247\t    text += \"\\n\\n\"\n   248\t\n   249\tprint(text)\n   250\t```\n   251\t\n   252\t### Add Watermark\n   253\t```python\n   254\tfrom pypdf import PdfReader, PdfWriter\n   255\t\n   256\t# Create watermark (or load existing)\n   257\twatermark = PdfReader(\"watermark.pdf\").pages[0]\n   258\t\n   259\t# Apply to all pages\n   260\treader = PdfReader(\"document.pdf\")\n   261\twriter = PdfWriter()\n   262\t\n Triggers include: any mention of 'Word doc', 'word document', '.docx', '.dotx', or requests to produce professional documents with formatting like tables of contents, page numbers, or letterheads. Also use when extracting or reorganizing content from .docx or .dotx files, inserting or replacing images in documents, find-and-replace in Word files, working with tracked changes or comments, or converting content into a polished Word document. If the user asks for a 'report', 'memo', 'letter', 'template', or similar deliverable as a Word or .docx file (to download, email or print), use this skill. However, if they ask for a document, page, report, memo, or notes WITHOUT naming a file format and the session offers a dedicated document or page skill or connector, use that instead. Do NOT use for PDFs, spreadsheets, Google Docs, or coding unrelated to document generation.\"\n     4\tlicense: Proprietary. LICENSE.txt has complete terms\n     5\t---\n     6\t\n     7\t# DOCX creation, editing, and analysis\n     8\t\n     9\tA `.docx` is a ZIP archive of XML files. Choose your approach by task:\n    10\t\n    11\t| Task | Approach |\n    12\t|---|---|\n    13\t| **Create** a new document | Write a `docx` (npm) script \u2014 see gotchas below |\n    14\t| **Edit** an existing document | `unzip` \u2192 edit `word/document.xml` \u2192 `zip` (docx-js cannot open existing files) |\n    15\t| **Read** content | `pandoc -t markdown file.docx` |\n    16\t\n    17\t> Script paths below are relative to this skill's directory.\n    18\t\n    19\t## Creating with docx-js \u2014 gotchas\n    20\t\n    21\t`docx` is preinstalled \u2014 do not run `npm install` first; write the script and `require('docx')` directly. Only if that require fails: `npm install docx`. The model knows the API; these are the footguns:\n    22\t\n    23\t- **Page size defaults to A4.** For US Letter set `page: { size: { width: 12240, height: 15840 } }` (DXA; 1440 = 1\u2033).\n    24\t- **Landscape:** pass portrait dimensions and `orientation: PageOrientation.LANDSCAPE` \u2014 docx-js swaps width/height internally.\n    25\t- **Tables need dual widths:** set `columnWidths` on the table AND `width` on every cell, both in `WidthType.DXA` (PERCENTAGE breaks in Google Docs). Column widths must sum to the table width.\n    26\t- **Table shading:** use `ShadingType.CLEAR`, never `SOLID` (renders black).\n    27\t- **Lists:** never insert `\u2022` literally; use a `numbering` config with `LevelFormat.BULLET`.\n    28\t- **`ImageRun` requires `type:`** (`\"png\"`, `\"jpg\"`, \u2026).\n    29\t- **`PageBreak` must be inside a `Paragraph`.**\n    30\t- **Never use `\\n`** \u2014 use separate `Paragraph` elements.\n    31\t- **TOC:** headings must use built-in `HeadingLevel.*`; custom heading styles need `outlineLevel` set or they won't appear.\n    32\t- **Don't use a table as a horizontal rule** \u2014 use a paragraph bottom border instead.\n    33\t- **Dot-leader / right-aligned-on-same-line:** use `PositionalTab` (`alignment: PositionalTabAlignment.RIGHT`, `leader: PositionalTabLeader.DOT`) inside a `TextRun`, not literal `.` or space padding.\n    34\t\n    35\t## Verify the output\n    36\t\n    37\tAfter writing a `.docx`, render it and look at it:\n    38\t\n    39\t```bash\n    40\tpython scripts/office/soffice.py --headless --convert-to pdf output.docx\n    41\tpdftoppm -jpeg -r 100 output.pdf page\n    42\tls page-*.jpg   # then Read the images\n    43\t```\n    44\t\n    45\t`pdftoppm` zero-pads page numbers to the width of the page count (`page-01.jpg`\u2026`page-12.jpg`).\n    46\t\n    47\t## Editing existing documents\n    48\t\n    49\tLegacy `.doc` files must be converted first: `python scripts/office/soffice.py --headless --convert-to docx file.doc`.\n    50\t\n    51\t```bash\n    52\tunzip -q doc.docx -d unpacked/\n    53\tfind unpacked -type l -delete   # strip symlink entries \u2014 docx from external parties is untrusted\n    54\tpython scripts/merge_runs.py unpacked/   # coalesce fragmented runs so text is findable\n    55\t# edit unpacked/word/document.xml in place \u2014 do NOT reformat or pretty-print\n    56\t(cd unpacked && rm -f ../out.docx && zip -Xr ../out.docx .)\n    57\tpython scripts/office/validate.py out.docx --original doc.docx   # XSD checks; --auto-repair fixes common issues\n    58\t# redlining? add --author \"<the name you redlined under>\" to check every edit is tracked\n    59\t```\n    60\t\n    61\tWord splits text across many `<w:r>` runs (revision ids, spell-check markers), so a phrase you can see in the document often doesn't exist as a contiguous string in the XML. `merge_runs.py` merges adjacent identically-formatted runs in `word/document.xml` without changing content or rendering; it also accepts a `.docx` directly (`python scripts/merge_runs.py doc.docx -o merged.docx`).\n    62\t\n    63\t**Tracked changes:** when redlining, validate with `--author \"<the name you redlined under>\"` (needs `--original`) \u2014 it reports any text you changed without a `<w:ins>`/`<w:del>` around it, which is easy to do by accident and invisible in the accepted view. Wrap runs in `<w:ins>`/`<w:del>` with `w:id`, `w:author`, `w:date` attributes. Inside `<w:del>`, the text element is `<w:delText>`, not `<w:t>`. A deleted paragraph mark (`<w:pPr><w:rPr><w:del w:id=\"..\" w:author=\"..\" w:date=\"..\"/></w:rPr></w:pPr>`) means \"merge this paragraph into the next\" \u2014 so deleting a paragraph outright is that plus a `<w:del>` around every run. The `<w:del/>` must come before the rPr's other children; their order is schema-enforced.\n    64\t\n    65\tTo produce a clean copy with all tracked changes accepted: `python scripts/accept_changes.py in.docx out.docx`.\n    66\t\n    67\tAccepting a deleted paragraph mark should join that paragraph to the one below it, so a paragraph whose runs are *all* deleted vanishes. Word does this; `accept_changes.py` and `pandoc --track-changes=accept` don't always. Both fail the same way \u2014 they strip the deleted text but leave the emptied paragraph behind, which reads as a stray empty bullet when it was auto-numbered:\n    68\t\n    69\t- `pandoc --track-changes=accept` never joins the paragraphs.\n    70\t- `accept_changes.py` (LibreOffice) joins them correctly, except when the deleted paragraph is followed by an empty spacer paragraph.\n    71\t\n    72\tAn empty bullet in either view is an artifact of that view, not a defect in the document. Check paragraph deletions in the XML.\n    73\t\n    74\t## Comments\n    75\t\n    76\tComments require six cross-linked files. Use the helper \u2014 directory mode when you'll also be editing `document.xml` (saves an unzip/rezip cycle), `.docx`-direct mode otherwise:\n    77\t\n    78\t```bash\n    79\t# Against an already-unpacked directory (preferred when also placing markers)\n    80\tpython scripts/comment.py unpacked/ \"Fees & expenses cap is too low\"\n    81\tpython scripts/comment.py unpacked/ \"Agreed\" --parent 0\n    82\t\n    83\t# Against a .docx directly\n    84\tpython scripts/comment.py contract.docx \"This cap is too low\" -o annotated.docx\n    85\t```\n    86\t\n    87\tThe script writes `comments.xml`, `commentsExtended.xml`, `commentsIds.xml`, `commentsExtensible.xml`, the relationships, and the content-type overrides. Comment IDs are auto-assigned. It then prints the `<w:commentRangeStart>`/`<w:commentRangeEnd>`/`<w:commentReference>` snippet to add to `word/document.xml` so the comment anchors to specific text \u2014 until you place those markers, the comment exists but is not visible.\n    88\t\n    89\t## Dependencies\n    90\t\n    91\t`docx` (npm, preinstalled \u2014 install only if `require('docx')` fails) \u00b7 `pandoc` \u00b7 LibreOffice (`soffice`) \u00b7 `pdftoppm` (Poppler)\n    92\t", "uuid": "d001e248-31cb-496a-b628-c73512e278a0"}], "is_error": false, "structured_content": null, "meta": {"output_format_category": Honours in Information Technology - Specialization in Data Science\r\nIT3101 \u2013 Data Warehousing and Business Intelligence\r\nLecture 05\r\nMr. Nadana Swasthi\r\nContent\r\n1. Data Integration Techniques\r\n2. Extracting data from various sources\r\n3. Incremental loading vs. full loading\r\n4. Data profiling and data quality assessment\r\nIT 3101 - DWBI 2\r\nWhat is Data Integration?\r\nData integration is the process of consolidating business information or data sets\r\nfrom various sources, which may be in different formats, and providing users with\r\na unified view of the data.\r\nThe objective is to create data that is:\r\n\u2022 Remove data silos\r\n\u2022 Improve data accessibility\r\n\u2022 Support enterprise-wide analysis\r\nIT 3101 - DWBI 3\r\nData Integration in a DW\r\nTraditional Architecture\r\nIT 3101 - DWBI 4\r\nOperational Data Store (ODS)\r\nAn ODS is an intermediate data storage layer between operational systems\r\nand the data warehouse.\r\nIt collects, integrates, and stores current operational data from multiple source\r\nsystems to provide a more consistent and up-to-date view of business information.\r\nAn ODS is needed in a DW architecture because it acts as a bridge between\r\noperational systems and the data warehouse, providing integrated and\r\ncurrent data for operational needs.\r\nThis will provide near real-time data access, integrate data from multiple sources,\r\nreduce workload on operational systems, clean and transform data before loading\r\ninto the DW, support operational reporting.\r\nIT 3101 - DWBI 5\r\nData Integration Techniques\r\nData Federation\r\nProvides a single virtual view of data from multiple heterogeneous\r\nsources without physically moving the data.\r\nData remains in the original source systems and is accessed on demand when a\r\nuser/application submits a query.\r\nA federation layer:\r\nRetrieves data from different sources\r\nIntegrates the results\r\nPerforms required transformations\r\ndynamically\r\nPresents a unified virtual schema\r\n(mediated schema) to users\r\nIT 3101 - DWBI 6\r\nData Integration Techniques\r\nData Propagation\r\nData propagation is an integration technique that copies data changes\r\nfrom a source system to one or more target systems.\r\nData is usually transferred online and can be:\r\n\u2022 Event-driven (changes trigger data movement)\r\n\u2022 Synchronous (source and target updated together)\r\n\u2022 Asynchronous (target updated after the source change)\r\nThis ensures that updates made in source systems are delivered to target systems\r\nand maintains consistency between distributed systems.\r\nImplementation Approaches\r\n\u2022 Enterprise Application Integration (EAI): Applications exchange and copy\r\ndata between systems.\r\n\u2022 Enterprise Data Replication (EDR) : Specialized mechanisms replicate data\r\nchanges between databases.\r\nIT 3101 - DWBI 7\r\nData Integration Techniques\r\nData Consolidation\r\nData consolidation integrates data from multiple source systems into a\r\nsingle persistent data repository.\r\nThe consolidated data store becomes a central source for:\r\nReporting and business intelligence\r\nData analysis and decision-making\r\nDownstream applications and analytics systems\r\nData is physically moved from source systems to a target repository and usually\r\ntransformed, cleaned, and integrated before analysis.\r\nUpdates may have a delay (data latency) depending on business requirements.\r\nBatch updates \u2192 hours/days\r\nNear real-time updates \u2192 seconds/minutes\r\nReal-time data \u2192 minimal latency\r\nIT 3101 - DWBI 8\r\nData Integration Techniques\r\nData consolidation creates a centralized, integrated data environment optimized for\r\nanalytics and reporting.\r\nIT 3101 - DWBI 9\r\nActivity\r\nA university has the following systems:\r\nStudent Information System Library Management System\r\nFinance System Learning Management System (LMS)\r\nThe university wants to create an analytics platform. For each requirement, decide\r\nthe most suitable approach:\r\nOptions:\r\nData Federation\r\nData Propagation\r\nData Consolidation\r\nIT 3101 - DWBI 10\r\nActivity\r\nQ1. The university wants a dashboard showing current student information\r\nwithout copying data into another database.\r\nQ2. The university wants to copy student payment updates immediately from\r\nFinance System to the reporting database.\r\nQ3. The university wants five years of student performance data for BI reports.\r\nIT 3101 - DWBI 11\r\nETL Process\r\nIT 3101 - DWBI 12\r\nETL at Several Levels\r\nMany ETL layers due to intermediate storage layers.\r\nIT 3101 - DWBI 13\r\nETL Considerations\r\nDifferent types of sources:\r\n\u2022 Database systems\r\n\u2022 Files (.csv, .txt, .xlsx, etc.)\r\n\u2022 Documents (JSON, XML, etc.)\r\n\u2022 Legacy systems\r\n\u2022 APIs\r\nData source connectivity and security concerns\r\nDifferent frequency requirements:\r\n\u2022 Near real-time, hourly, daily, weekly, etc.\r\nIT 3101 - DWBI 14\r\nETL Considerations\r\nExtraction window limitations:\r\n\u2022 Small time frames to cater near real time requirements\r\n\u2022 Probably off-peak times for scheduled batch extractions\r\nSource data realities\r\n\u2022 Data quality issues\r\n\u2022 Extraction window limitations\r\n\u2022Capabilities of tools used\r\n\u2022 Support of traditional ETL tools for real-time extractions\r\nIT 3101 - DWBI 15\r\nData Extraction\r\nData extraction is the process of retrieving data from source systems for processing\r\nand integration.\r\nIT 3101 - DWBI 16\r\nCommon Extraction Methods\r\nDatabase Extraction\r\nUsing queries:\r\nSELECT *\r\nFROM Sales;\r\nFile Extraction\r\nExamples:\r\nCSV files\r\nExcel files\r\nXML files\r\nIT 3101 - DWBI 17\r\nAPI Extraction\r\nApplication REST API DW\r\nFull vs Incremental Extraction\r\nFull Extraction\r\n\u2022 Extracts the complete dataset from the source system and loading it into the\r\nData Warehouse every time.\r\n\u2022 It is simple to implement and ensures all data is refreshed, but it requires more\r\nprocessing time and resources.\r\nIncremental Extraction\r\n\u2022 Extracts only the new or modified data since the last extraction.\r\n\u2022 It improves performance, reduces resource usage, and is commonly used for\r\nregular ETL updates in large Data Warehouses.\r\nIT 3101 - DWBI 18\r\nPhysical Extraction Methods\r\nOnline Extraction\r\nData is extracted directly from the\r\nsource system itself.\r\n\u2022 Direct access to operational systems\r\n\u2022 Data can be extracted in real-time or\r\nnear real-time\r\n\u2022 No intermediate storage is required\r\n\u2022 Example: Extracting data directly\r\nfrom a database using SQL queries\r\nIT 3101 - DWBI 19\r\nOffline Extraction\r\nData is first staged outside the original\r\nsource system before extraction.\r\n\u2022 Source system pushes data into\r\nseparate storage\r\n\u2022 Extraction process accesses the\r\nstaged data\r\n\u2022 Common formats:\r\n\u2022 Flat files (CSV, TXT)\r\n\u2022 Database dump files\r\n\u2022 Usually used for batch data\r\nextraction\r\nPush vs Pull Data Extraction\r\nPush Extraction\r\nThe source system sends data to the target system without the target\r\nrequesting it.\r\nSource system creates a snapshot of changes and delivers it to downstream\r\nsystems.\r\nCommonly used with:\r\n\u2022 Incremental extraction\r\n\u2022 Offline extraction\r\nSuitable when the source system controls when data becomes available.\r\nExample: A sales system exports daily transaction changes into a CSV file and\r\nsends it to the data warehouse.\r\nIT 3101 - DWBI 20\r\nSource\r\nSystem\r\nStaging Area /\r\nData\r\nWarehouse\r\nSends data changes\r\nPush vs Pull Data Extraction\r\nPull Extraction\r\nThe target system requests and retrieves data from the source system.\r\nThe extraction process connects to the source system and retrieves required data.\r\nCommonly used with:\r\n\u2022 Online extraction\r\nCan support:\r\nFull extraction\r\nIncremental extraction\r\nExample: A data warehouse queries a CRM database every night to retrieve newly\r\nupdated customer records.\r\nIT 3101 - DWBI 21\r\nData\r\nWarehouse\r\nSource\r\nSystem\r\nRequest data\r\nActivity\r\nA supermarket wants to load sales data into a data warehouse.\r\nCurrent system:\r\nSales Database\r\n500 million transactions\r\n100,000 new transactions/day\r\n\u2022 Would you use Full extraction or Incremental extraction?\r\n\u2022 The sales system automatically exports daily transaction files. Is this:\r\nPush or Pull\r\nIT 3101 - DWBI 22\r\nData Profiling and Data Quality Assessment\r\nIT 3101 - DWBI 23\r\nData Profiling\r\nData profiling is the process of analysing datasets to understand their structure,\r\ncontent, and quality.\r\nBefore loading data into a warehouse, we need to know:\r\n\u2022 What values exist?\r\n\u2022 Are there missing values?\r\n\u2022 Are there duplicates?\r\n\u2022 Are values valid?\r\nIT 3101 - DWBI 24\r\nCore Data Profiling Activities\r\nColumn Profiling: Scans individual fields to check data types, lengths, null\r\ncounts, unique values, and frequency distributions.\r\nStatistical Analysis: Gathers basic metrics like minimum, maximum, mean,\r\nmode, median, and standard deviation to see value ranges.\r\nCross-Column Profiling: Evaluates data across multiple columns in a single\r\ntable to find dependencies and test for primary key candidates.\r\nCross-Table Profiling: Analyzes relationships between different tables, using\r\nforeign keys to check for missing links or orphaned records.\r\nData Rule Validation: Tests if data values match specific business rules, formats,\r\nor regulatory requirements.\r\nPattern Discovery: Identifies recurring text patterns, such as phone numbers,\r\ndates, or postal codes, to spot format errors.\r\nIT 3101 - DWBI 25\r\nIT 3101 - DWBI 26\r\nData Quality Dimensions\r\nIT 3101 - DWBI 27\r\nData Quality Assessment Example\r\nIT 3101 - DWBI 28\r\nID Name Age Country\r\n1 John 35 Sri Lanka\r\n2 John 35 LK\r\n3 Sara -5 Sri Lanka\r\n4 NULL 40 NULL\r\nNext Lecture\r\n1. Data transformation and cleansing\r\n2. Loading data into the data warehouse\r\n3. Incremental loading vs. full loading\r\n4. Change Data Capture (CDC) techniques\r\n5.
